Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a pervasive 'lookback mechanism' that language models use to track characters' beliefs, and introduces the CausalToM dataset for causal analysis of Theory of Mind.
papers.conclusion: The lookback mechanism is a foundational computation for belief tracking in language models, providing a step toward reverse-engineering Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Language models use a systematic 'lookback mechanism' for belief tracking, which involves recalling important information when needed.
The mechanism uses Ordering IDs (OIs) to bind character-object-state triples in the residual stream of state tokens.
Three key lookbacks are identified: binding lookback (retrieves state OI), answer lookback (retrieves state token), and visibility lookback (updates beliefs based on visibility).
The mechanism generalizes across model scales (70B to 405B) and model families (Llama and Qwen).
The visibility lookback uses a visibility ID to retrieve information about observed characters and update the observing character's beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The visibility lookback mechanism is only partially understood and requires further investigation.
The mechanism does not scale to three characters in the visibility condition.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex scenarios with more characters and objects.
Further investigation of the visibility lookback mechanism.
Applying the lookback mechanism analysis to other tasks and domains.
papers.abstract: How do language models (LMs) represent characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality? This question lies at the heart of understanding the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LMs. We analyze LMs' ability to reason about characters' beliefs using causal mediation and abstraction. We construct a dataset, CausalToM, consisting of simple stories where two characters independently change the state of two objects, potentially unaware of each other's actions. Our investigation uncovers a pervasive algorithmic pattern that we call a lookback mechanism, which enables the LM to recall important information when it becomes necessary. The LM binds each character-object-state triple together by co-locating their reference information, represented as Ordering IDs (OIs), in low-rank subspaces of the state token's residual stream. When asked about a character's beliefs regarding the state of an object, the binding lookback retrieves the correct state OI and then the answer lookback retrieves the corresponding state token. When we introduce text specifying that one character is (not) visible to the other, we find that the LM first generates a visibility ID encoding the relation between the observing and the observed character OIs. In a visibility lookback, this ID is used to retrieve information about the observed character and update the observing character's beliefs. Our work provides insights into belief tracking mechanisms, taking a step toward reverse-engineering ToM reasoning in LMs.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Illustrating a neural model of logic computations: The case of Sherlock Holmes' old maxim
papers.research_question: What is the cognitive reason for the feeling that Holmes' maxim is an evident truth? The paper postulates that it is because our brains have neural modules that perform modal logical computations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a neural model based on matrix associative memories that can perform modal logical computations, explaining why humans accept Sherlock Holmes' maxim as true.
papers.conclusion: Our brains are equipped with neural modules capable of modal logical computations, which explains why we accept Holmes' maxim as true.
papers.key_findings:
The paper provides a neural model based on matrix associative memories that can perform logical operations.
It shows how modal logic operators (possibility and necessity) can be implemented in the model.
It demonstrates how Holmes' maxim can be represented and computed by the model.
It connects the model with subjective probabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical approach helps explain cognitive acceptability, but mathematics itself remains unexplained, making the explanation incomplete and provisional.
The link between cognitive probabilities and formal probabilities is left as an open problem.
future_direction: Exploring whether the process represents a class of nonmonotonic reasoning.
Investigating the link between cognitive probabilities and formal probabilities.
papers.abstract: Natural languages can express some logical propositions that humans are able to understand. We illustrate this fact with a famous text that Conan Doyle attributed to Holmes: 'It is an old maxim of mine that when you have excluded the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth'. This is a subtle logical statement usually felt as an evident truth. The problem we are trying to solve is the cognitive reason for such a feeling. We postulate here that we accept Holmes' maxim as true because our adult brains are equipped with neural modules that naturally perform modal logical computations.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Adaptive Activation Steering: A Tuning-Free LLM Truthfulness Improvement Method for Diverse Hallucinations Categories
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to improve the truthfulness of large language models by adaptively steering activations during inference, addressing the gap between what the model knows and what it tells, and handling diverse hallucination categories.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Adaptive Activation Steering (ACT), a tuning-free method that improves LLM truthfulness by adaptively shifting activations toward truthful directions using diverse steering vectors and adaptive intensity control.
papers.conclusion: ACT is a tuning-free method that enhances LLM truthfulness by steering activations with diverse vectors and adaptive intensity, effectively addressing the gap between knowing and telling, and marks a promising advancement in reliable AI-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
ACT significantly improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA across multiple models (e.g., LLaMA, LLaMA2, Alpaca, Vicuna, LLaMA2-Chat, LLaMA3).
ACT's adaptive intensity control and diverse steering vectors are effective, outperforming existing baselines like ITI, CCS, RepE, and Mean-Centring.
ACT is orthogonal to few-shot prompting and instruction fine-tuning, and can be combined with them for further improvement.
ACT shows scalability across model sizes (7B to 65B), with consistent improvements.
ACT requires only a few dozen training samples and adds constant-time complexity during inference.
papers.limitation:
Applicability in real-world chat settings involving multi-turn conversations has not been fully explored.
The trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness (e.g., the smoothness of generated text) is not explored.
future_direction: Explore ACT in multi-turn conversation settings.
Investigate the trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have indicated that Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor an inherent understanding of truthfulness, yet often fail to consistently express it and generate false statements. This gap between "knowing" and "telling" poses a challenge for ensuring the truthfulness of generated content. Inspired by recent work on the practice of encoding human-interpretable concepts linearly within large language models, we treat truthfulness as a specially linearly encoded concept within LLMs, and introduce Adaptive Activation Steering (ACT), a tuning-free method that adaptively shifts LLM's activations in the "truthful" direction during inference. ACT addresses diverse categories of hallucinations by utilizing diverse truthfulness-related steering vectors and adjusting the steering intensity adaptively. Applied as an add-on across various models, ACT significantly improves truthfulness in LLaMA ($\uparrow$ 142%), LLaMA2 ($\uparrow$ 24%), Alpaca ($\uparrow$ 36%), Vicuna ($\uparrow$ 28%), LLaMA2-Chat ($\uparrow$ 19%), and LLaMA3($\uparrow$ 34%). Furthermore, we verify ACT's scalability across larger models (13B, 33B, 65B), underscoring the adaptability of ACT to large-scale language models. Our code is available at https://github.com/tianlwang/ACT.

papers.title: Attention Sinks: A 'Catch, Tag, Release' Mechanism for Embeddings
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why attention sinks emerge in later tokens, whether they encode semantically meaningful information, how they differ between pretrained and reasoning models, and the impact of query-key normalization on attention sinks.
papers.core_contribution: This paper uncovers the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism in LLMs, where attention sinks catch tokens, tag them with semantically meaningful information, and release the tags into the residual stream for later use. The mechanism is prevalent across model families, more pronounced in reasoning models, and persists despite query-key normalization.
papers.conclusion: This work uncovers and formalizes the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism mediated by attention sinks, showing that sinks implement a functional tagging system that propagates semantically meaningful information across tokens, offering a foundation for deeper mechanistic investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Attention sinks implement a 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, where sinks catch tokens, tag them with a common direction, and release the tags into the residual stream.
Tags encode semantically meaningful information, such as the truth value of statements, as shown by probing experiments.
Reasoning-distilled models exhibit the mechanism more strongly, with more attention sinks and higher variance explained by tags.
Attention sinks remain prevalent in models with query-key normalization, despite the normalization's intended effect.
The mechanism can emerge through training in a minimal theoretical model designed to solve a sequence averaging task.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical model does not prove the mechanism is necessary and may not reflect real-world complexity.
The threshold-based metric for identifying attention sinks may not capture all such tokens and lacks a principled method for setting the threshold.
The connection between the mechanism and reasoning is suggestive but not causally established.
future_direction: Deeper mechanistic investigations into token interactions and the role of implicit memory in transformers.
Establishing a causal link between the mechanism and reasoning.
Exploring practical applications such as steering activations for alignment and safety, and preserving the mechanism in model compression.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often concentrate their attention on a few specific tokens referred to as attention sinks. Common examples include the first token, a prompt-independent sink, and punctuation tokens, which are prompt-dependent. While the tokens causing the sinks often lack direct semantic meaning, the presence of the sinks is critical for model performance, particularly under model compression and KV-caching. Despite their ubiquity, the function, semantic role, and origin of attention sinks -- especially those beyond the first token -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation demonstrating that attention sinks: catch a sequence of tokens, tag them using a common direction in embedding space, and release them back into the residual stream, where tokens are later retrieved based on the tags they have acquired. Probing experiments reveal these tags carry semantically meaningful information, such as the truth of a statement. These findings extend to reasoning models, where the mechanism spans more heads and explains greater variance in embeddings, or recent models with query-key normalization, where sinks remain just as prevalent. To encourage future theoretical analysis, we introduce a minimal problem which can be solved through the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, and where it emerges through training.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Decoding Knowledge in Large Language Models: A Framework for Categorization and Comprehension
papers.research_question: How can we categorize and analyze the knowledge in large language models by considering both correctness and confidence, and how do techniques like chain-of-thought prompting and instruction tuning affect this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the K-(CSA)² framework for categorizing LLM knowledge along dimensions of correctness and confidence, enabling a nuanced evaluation beyond binary accuracy and revealing how techniques like CoT and instruction tuning alter knowledge structures.
papers.conclusion: The K-(CSA)² framework provides systematic metrics for assessing LLMs' knowledge structures by evaluating correctness and confidence, revealing novel patterns in how knowledge is organized and evolves, which can benefit future model development.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models are more assertive regardless of correctness, showing higher confidence in both correct and incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting creates synergistic benefits when combined with instruction tuning, improving both accuracy and category scores.
Instruction-tuned models show superior context understanding for external knowledge, with IT+CoT providing complementary benefits.
Higher layers in LLMs encode more high-confidence knowledge, while low-confidence knowledge tends to emerge in middle-to-lower layers.
Rising accuracy during pre-training does not guarantee better knowledge structure, as category scores can initially decrease before improving.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on sampling to determine confidence levels, where the number of samples and temperature settings could affect categorization results.
The boundaries between categories, especially for 'Maybe Known' and 'Weakly Known', can sometimes be ambiguous.
Evaluating models through multiple sampling runs is computationally intensive, which may limit the framework's applicability in resource-constrained scenarios.
Evaluation primarily focuses on factual knowledge in question-answering contexts and may need adaptation for other types of knowledge or tasks.
For external knowledge evaluation, the framework doesn't fully capture how models integrate multiple pieces of context or handle conflicting information.
future_direction: Exploring sampling robustness and strengthening theoretical foundations for category boundaries.
Extending the framework to more complex scenarios beyond factual QA.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and apply knowledge remains an open challenge. This paper introduces a novel framework, K-(CSA)^2, which categorizes LLM knowledge along two dimensions: correctness and confidence. The framework defines six categories of knowledge, ranging from highly confident correctness to confidently held misconceptions, enabling a nuanced evaluation of model comprehension beyond binary accuracy. Using this framework, we demonstrate how techniques like chain-of-thought prompting and reinforcement learning with human feedback fundamentally alter the knowledge structures of internal (pre-trained) and external (context-dependent) knowledge in LLMs. CoT particularly enhances base model performance and shows synergistic benefits when applied to aligned LLMs. Moreover, our layer-wise analysis reveals that higher layers in LLMs encode more high-confidence knowledge, while low-confidence knowledge tends to emerge in middle-to-lower layers.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Attention Satisfies: A Constraint-Satisfaction Lens on Factual Errors of Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) internally behave when they generate factually incorrect text, and can attention to constraint tokens predict factual errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a strong positive relationship between an LLM's attention to constraint tokens and the factual accuracy of its generations. It proposes SAT Probe, a method that probes attention patterns to predict factual errors and constraint satisfaction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention patterns in LLMs provide a reliable signal for predicting factual errors, contributing to the mechanistic understanding of LLMs and offering a pathway to enhance their reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention to constraint tokens strongly correlates with the factual correctness of LLM generations.
SAT Probe, a linear probe on attention weights, can predict factual errors comparably to the model's own confidence score.
Larger LLMs tend to pay more attention to constraint tokens and achieve higher factual accuracy.
The total attention contribution from constraints across layers can be used to predict LLM success on factual queries.
Attention patterns can be used for early error identification, potentially stopping costly generation early.
papers.limitation: Exact match is used as a strict verification criterion for single-constraint queries, which could introduce noise to evaluations.
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal behavior of Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) when they generate factually incorrect text. We propose modeling factual queries as constraint satisfaction problems and use this framework to investigate how the LLM interacts internally with factual constraints. We find a strong positive relationship between the LLM's attention to constraint tokens and the factual accuracy of generations. We curate a suite of 10 datasets containing over 40,000 prompts to study the task of predicting factual errors with the Llama-2 family across all scales (7B, 13B, 70B). We propose SAT Probe, a method probing attention patterns, that can predict factual errors and fine-grained constraint satisfaction, and allow early error identification. The approach and findings take another step towards using the mechanistic understanding of LLMs to enhance their reliability.

papers.title: Simulated Adoption: Decoupling Magnitude and Direction in LLM In-Context Conflict Resolution
papers.research_question: Does the suppression of parametric knowledge in the residual stream arise from the radial dilution of the signal's magnitude, or from an angular displacement induced by orthogonal interference?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs resolve in-context knowledge conflicts through orthogonal interference in the residual stream, rotating hidden states rather than diluting signal magnitude, challenging scalar confidence metrics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs resolve knowledge conflicts via orthogonal interference in the residual stream, simulating adoption without erasing internal knowledge, highlighting the need for vectorial monitoring over scalar metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Logit decay for correct tokens occurs under conflicting contexts, most pronounced in final layers.
Norm dynamics vary by architecture; Llama-3.1-8B shows dilution, but Qwen-3-4B and GLM-4-9B maintain stable norms.
Interference vectors are quasi-orthogonal to truth directions, supporting the orthogonal interference hypothesis.
Angular deviation correlates strongly with performance drop, indicating geometric rotation is the dominant mechanism.
Compliance is characterized by simulated adoption, where internal truth is bypassed, not erased.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, assuming truth and context interact as linear vectors.
Dataset scope restricted to fact-based QA tasks (MMLU), may not generalize to other tasks.
Focus on final residual state before unembedding, not layer-wise evolution of interference vectors.
Sample size of three architectures may not capture behaviors of larger or MoE models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently prioritize conflicting in-context information over pre-existing parametric memory, a phenomenon often termed sycophancy or compliance. However, the mechanistic realization of this behavior remains obscure, specifically how the model resolves these knowledge conflicts through compliance, and whether this suppression arises from signal magnitude dilution or directional geometric alteration within the residual stream. To resolve this, we conducted a layer-wise geometric analysis across Qwen-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GLM-4-9B, decomposing the residual stream updates induced by counter-factual contexts into radial (norm-based) and angular (cosine-based) components. Our empirical results reject the universality of the "Manifold Dilution" hypothesis, as two of the three architectures maintained stable residual norms despite exhibiting significant performance degradation on factual queries. Instead, we observed that compliance is consistently characterized by "Orthogonal Interference," where the conflicting context injects a steering vector that is quasi-orthogonal to the ground-truth direction, effectively rotating the hidden state representation. This suggests that models do not "unlearn" or suppress the magnitude of internal truths but rather employ a mechanism of geometric displacement to bypass the correct unembedding vector, effectively simulating adoption while preserving the original structural magnitude. These findings challenge scalar confidence metrics for detecting hallucinations and underscore the necessity of vectorial monitoring to distinguish between genuine knowledge integration and superficial in-context mimicry.

papers.title: Cutting Off the Head Ends the Conflict: A Mechanism for Interpreting and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism of knowledge conflicts in language models, and how can they be mitigated by precise interventions at the pivotal point?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that knowledge conflicts in language models arise from the integration of inconsistent information flows by memory heads and context heads in later layers, and proposes a parameter-free method (PH3) to mitigate conflicts by pruning these heads.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a mechanistic interpretation of knowledge conflicts in LMs and demonstrates that the proposed PH3 method can effectively mitigate these conflicts and control model behavior, showing strong generalization across models, relations, and data formats.
papers.key_findings:
FFNs in early layers enrich the semantic information of input elements, while MHAs in middle and late layers are crucial for passing information to the last token.
The last token extracts attribute information from the context subject (internal memory) and context attribute (external context) in later layers.
Some attention heads in late MHAs play opposite roles: memory heads recall knowledge from internal memory, and context heads retrieve knowledge from external context.
The pivotal point of knowledge conflict is the integration of inconsistent information flows by memory heads and context heads.
The proposed PH3 method can flexibly control LMs to use internal memory (↑44.0%) or external context (↑38.5%) by pruning conflicting attention heads without updating parameters.

papers.title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts?
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs genuinely believe facts implanted via knowledge editing techniques, and develops a framework to measure the depth of such beliefs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to measure belief depth in LLMs for implanted facts, operationalized through generality, robustness, and internal representations. It finds that Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) often implants beliefs deeply, while prompting and mechanistic editing fail.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that measuring belief depth is crucial for evaluating knowledge editing, and while SDF can implant deep beliefs, its effectiveness varies with fact plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting and mechanistic editing fail to implant knowledge deeply; beliefs are not robust and have internal representations distinct from genuine knowledge.
Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) often succeeds in implanting beliefs that generalize to related contexts, are robust to scrutiny, and have similar internal representations to genuine knowledge.
SDF's success depends on fact plausibility; implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct.
Implanted beliefs from SDF are robust to increased inference-time compute, with minimal impact on belief rates.
Internal representations of SDF-implanted facts resemble genuine knowledge for plausible facts, but adversarial probes can distinguish implausible ones.
papers.limitation: SDF's success is not universal; implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct.
future_direction: Continued evaluation of SDF on highly capable future systems
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing techniques promise to implant new factual knowledge into large language models (LLMs). But do LLMs really believe these facts? We develop a framework to measure belief depth and use it to evaluate the success of knowledge editing techniques. We operationalize belief depth as the extent to which implanted knowledge 1) generalizes to related contexts (e.g. Fermi estimates several logical steps removed), 2) is robust to self-scrutiny and direct challenge, and 3) is represented similarly to genuine knowledge (as measured by linear probes). Our evaluations show that simple prompting and mechanistic editing techniques fail to implant knowledge deeply. In contrast, Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) - where models are trained on LLM-generated documents consistent with a fact - often succeeds at implanting beliefs that behave similarly to genuine knowledge. However, SDF's success is not universal, as implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct from genuine knowledge. Overall, our work introduces measurable criteria for belief depth and enables the rigorous evaluation necessary for deploying knowledge editing in real-world applications.

papers.title: A Language Model with Limited Memory Capacity Captures Interference in Human Sentence Processing
papers.research_question: Can a neural language model with limited memory capacity (single self-attention head) capture similarity-based interference effects (semantic and syntactic) observed in human sentence processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a recurrent neural language model with a single self-attention head (CBR-RNN) that integrates expectation and memory-based theories of sentence processing, and shows that its attention mechanism captures semantic and syntactic interference effects observed in human experiments.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that mechanistic explanations of processing difficulty rooted in memory retrieval constraints can emerge as a by-product of minimizing the surprisal of upcoming words in a language model with limited memory capacity.
papers.key_findings:
The CBR-RNN's single attention head tracks subject-verb dependencies over long distances and with intervening nouns, without direct supervision.
The model captures both agreement attraction and semantic attraction effects, as measured by relative attention and surprisal.
In double violation conditions, the effects of agreement and semantic attraction are additive, consistent with human data.
Surprisal estimates from the model also capture the attraction effects, providing a unified account of expectation and memory-based processing difficulty.
Compared to GPT-2, which requires identifying specialized attention heads, the single-head model provides a simpler and more cognitively plausible measure of interference.
papers.limitation:
Only subject-verb dependencies were investigated; other dependency types (e.g., reflexive anaphora, filler-gap) remain for future work.
The model assumes working memory items are representations of previous timesteps, whereas cue-based retrieval theories typically assume syntactic constituents.
It is unclear whether the model learns interpretable linguistic features (e.g., [+/-subject]) that are posited by cognitive theories.
Training data is Wikipedia text, which is not developmentally plausible and lacks multimodal experience.
future_direction: Evaluate the model on various dependency types, such as reflexive anaphora and filler-gap dependencies.
Incorporate syntactic attention masking to explicitly represent syntactic structure in memory.
Investigate whether training on developmentally-plausible corpora (e.g., child-directed speech) leads to more humanlike memory retrieval behaviors.
papers.abstract: Two of the central factors believed to underpin human sentence processing difficulty are expectations and retrieval from working memory. A recent attempt to create a unified cognitive model integrating these two factors have relied on the parallels between the self-attention mechanism of transformer language models and cue-based retrieval theories of working memory in human sentence processing (Ryu and Lewis 2021). While the authors show that attention patterns in specialized attention heads of GPT-2 are consistent with a key prediction of cue-based retrieval models, similarity-based interference effects, their method requires the identification of syntactically specialized attention heads, and makes an cognitively implausible implicit assumption that hundreds of memory retrieval operations take place in parallel. In the present work, we develop a recurrent neural language model with a single self-attention head, which more closely parallels the memory system assumed by cognitive theories. We show that our model's single attention head can capture semantic and syntactic interference effects observed in human experiments.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Pre-training Limited Memory Language Models with Internal and External Knowledge
papers.research_question: Can factual memorization be disentangled from language understanding in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Limited Memory Language Models (LMLM), a pre-training method that externalizes factual knowledge to an external database, disentangling knowledge from language understanding and enabling editable and verifiable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMLMs offer a pathway toward language models with substantially reduced dependency on parameter count for factual accuracy and enable precise control over factual knowledge through an external database.
papers.key_findings:
LMLMs achieve lower perplexity than standard models of the same size during pre-training.
LMLMs improve factual precision over standard models and approach the performance of much larger models.
LMLMs support instant unlearning by simply removing database entries, without degrading model utility.
LMLMs learn to generate lookup calls effectively and rely on the external database for facts.
LMLMs do not compromise general language understanding capabilities, as shown by NLU benchmark performance.
papers.limitation:
Incur upfront costs for data annotation and model training.
Currently focuses on entity-level atomic facts; extending to more complex knowledge structures is future work.
future_direction: Extend LMLM to more complex knowledge structures beyond entity-level facts.
Integrate LMLM with symbolic reasoning and knowledge representation.
Scale LMLM to larger models and databases.
papers.abstract: Neural language models are black-boxes--both linguistic patterns and factual knowledge are distributed across billions of opaque parameters. This entangled encoding makes it difficult to reliably inspect, verify, or update specific facts. We introduce Limited Memory Language Models (LMLM), a new class of language models that externalizes factual knowledge to external database during pre-training rather than memorizing them. Our pre-training approach strategically masks externally retrieved factual values from the training loss, thereby teaching the model to perform targeted lookups rather than relying on memorization in model weights. Our experiments demonstrate that LMLMs achieve competitive performance compared to significantly larger LLMs on standard benchmarks, while offering the advantages of explicit, editable, and verifiable knowledge bases.

papers.title: Linearity of Relation Decoding in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models represent and decode relational knowledge? Is the decoding process for relations linear?
papers.core_contribution: For a subset of relations, transformer language models decode relational knowledge via a linear transformation on the subject representation, which can be estimated from the model's Jacobian.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models employ linear relational embeddings for a subset of relations, revealing a simple, interpretable, but heterogeneously deployed knowledge representation strategy.
papers.key_findings:
For 48% of the relations tested, the relation decoding is well-approximated by a linear relational embedding (LRE).
LREs can be estimated from the model's Jacobian using a few examples and are causally involved in the model's predictions.
Some relations are not linearly decodable, indicating that LMs use heterogeneous knowledge representation strategies.
The attribute lens, built from LREs, visualizes relational knowledge in intermediate layers and can reveal latent knowledge.
LREs can be used to edit subject representations to control model output, demonstrating causal influence.
papers.limitation:
The dataset only includes 47 relations, limiting the generality of the findings.
Evaluation uses first-token correctness, which may lead to false positives when multiple objects share the same first token.
The dataset assumes a single correct object per subject, but some relations may have multiple correct answers.
future_direction: Extending the method to multi-token objects and relations with multiple correct answers.
Applying LREs to mitigate biases in models.
papers.abstract: Much of the knowledge encoded in transformer language models (LMs) may be expressed in terms of relations: relations between words and their synonyms, entities and their attributes, etc. We show that, for a subset of relations, this computation is well-approximated by a single linear transformation on the subject representation. Linear relation representations may be obtained by constructing a first-order approximation to the LM from a single prompt, and they exist for a variety of factual, commonsense, and linguistic relations. However, we also identify many cases in which LM predictions capture relational knowledge accurately, but this knowledge is not linearly encoded in their representations. Our results thus reveal a simple, interpretable, but heterogeneously deployed knowledge representation strategy in transformer LMs.

papers.title: If Attention Serves as a Cognitive Model of Human Memory Retrieval, What is the Plausible Memory Representation?
papers.research_question: Investigates whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Transformer Grammar's attention, operating on syntactic structures, better predicts human reading times than vanilla Transformer, suggesting dual memory representations in human sentence processing with attention as a general memory retrieval algorithm.
papers.conclusion: Attention can serve as the general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from two representational systems, and Transformer Grammar, with its syntactic structure-based attention, best captures dominant factors in human sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
TG's NAE has stronger predictive power for reading times than Transformer's NAE.
TG's and Transformer's NAE have independent contributions to reading time prediction, suggesting they capture distinct aspects of memory retrieval.
TG's NAE captures interference effects, independent of decay effects modeled by Category Locality Theory.
TG's advantage over TG−comp indicates the importance of treating closed phrases as single representations (via COMPOSE attention) for capturing syntax-based memory retrieval.
The attention mechanism serves as a general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from dual representational systems (syntactic and token-based).
papers.limitation:
The NAE calculation procedure (summing across heads, handling subwords) strictly followed Oh and Schuler (2022), but alternative approaches warrant investigation.
The findings are based on the English Natural Stories corpus; generalizability to other languages and cognitive measures (e.g., gaze duration, EEG) remains to be investigated.
The use of 'perfect oracles' for syntactic structures idealizes away from local ambiguities that humans encounter during actual sentence processing.
future_direction: Incorporate more realistic elements such as parallel parsing, left-corner parsing strategies, and memory decay mechanisms to fully operate at the algorithmic level.
Investigate generalizability to different languages and other measures of cognitive load.
Explore alternative approaches to handling layers, attention heads, and subword tokens in NAE calculation.
papers.abstract: Recent work in computational psycholinguistics has revealed intriguing parallels between attention mechanisms and human memory retrieval, focusing primarily on vanilla Transformers that operate on token-level representations. However, computational psycholinguistic research has also established that syntactic structures provide compelling explanations for human sentence processing that token-level factors cannot fully account for. In this paper, we investigate whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis between models and humans. Our experiments demonstrate that TG's attention achieves superior predictive power for self-paced reading times compared to vanilla Transformer's, with further analyses revealing independent contributions from both models. These findings suggest that human sentence processing involves dual memory representations -- one based on syntactic structures and another on token sequences -- with attention serving as the general memory retrieval algorithm, while highlighting the importance of incorporating syntactic structures as representational units.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Separating the Brain Regions Involved in Recollection and Familiarity in Recognition Memory
papers.abstract: The neural substrates of recognition memory retrieval were examined in a functional magnetic resonance imaging study designed to separate activity related to recollection from that related to continuous variations in familiarity. Across a variety of brain regions, the neural signature of recollection was found to be distinct from familiarity, demonstrating that recollection cannot be attributed to familiarity strength. In the prefrontal cortex, an anterior medial region was related to recollection, but lateral regions, including the anterior and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, were related to familiarity. Along the lateral parietal cortex, two functionally distinct regions were also observed: a lateral parietal/temporal region related to recollection and a more superior parietal region involved in familiarity. Similarly, in medial parietal regions, the posterior cingulate was related to recollection, whereas the precuneus was related to familiarity. The hippocampus was related to recollection, but also exhibited an inverse relationship to familiarity-driven recognition confidence. The results indicate that recollection and familiarity rely on different networks of brain regions and provide insights into the functional roles of different regions involved in episodic recognition memory.

papers.title: Recollection and Familiarity in Recognition Memory: An Event-Related Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study
papers.abstract: The question of whether recognition memory judgments with and without recollection reflect dissociable patterns of brain activity is unresolved. We used event-related, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) of 12 healthy volunteers to measure hemodynamic responses associated with both studying and recognizing words. Volunteers made one of three judgments to each word during recognition: whether they recollected seeing it during study (R judgments), whether they experienced a feeling of familiarity in the absence of recollection (K judgments), or whether they did not remember seeing it during study (N judgments). Both R and K judgments for studied words were associated with enhanced responses in left prefrontal and left parietal cortices relative to N judgments for unstudied words. The opposite pattern was observed in bilateral temporoccipital regions and amygdalae. R judgments for studied words were associated with enhanced responses in anterior left prefrontal, left parietal, and posterior cingulate regions relative to K judgments. At study, a posterior left prefrontal region exhibited an enhanced response to words subsequently given R versus K judgments, but the response of this region during recognition did not differentiate R and K judgments. K judgments for studied words were associated with enhanced responses in right lateral and medial prefrontal cortex relative to both R judgments for studied words and N judgments for unstudied words, a difference we attribute to greater monitoring demands when memory judgments are less certain. These results suggest that the responses of different brain regions do dissociate according to the phenomenology associated with memory retrieval.

papers.title: Causal Evidence for Mnemonic Metacognition in Human Precuneus
papers.abstract: Metacognition is the capacity to introspectively monitor and control one's own cognitive processes. Previous anatomical and functional neuroimaging findings implicated the important role of the precuneus in metacognition processing, especially during mnemonic tasks. However, the issue of whether this medial parietal cortex is a domain-specific region that supports mnemonic metacognition remains controversial. Here, we focally disrupted this parietal area with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in healthy human participants of both sexes, seeking to ascertain its functional necessity for metacognition in memory versus perceptual decisions. Perturbing precuneal activity selectively impaired metacognitive efficiency of temporal-order memory judgment, but not perceptual discrimination. Moreover, the correlation in individuals' metacognitive efficiency between domains disappeared when the precuneus was perturbed. Together, these findings provide evidence reinforcing the notion that the precuneal region plays an important role in mediating metacognition of episodic memory retrieval.SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT Theories on the neural basis of metacognition have thus far been largely centered on the role of the prefrontal cortex. Here we refined the theoretical framework through characterizing a unique precuneal involvement in mnemonic metacognition with a noninvasive but inferentially powerful method: transcranial magnetic stimulation. By quantifying metacognitive efficiency across two distinct domains (memory vs perception) that are matched for stimulus characteristics, we reveal an instrumental role of the precuneus in mnemonic metacognition. This causal evidence corroborates ample clinical reports that parietal lobe lesions often produce inaccurate self-reports of confidence in memory recollection and establish the precuneus as a nexus for the introspective ability to evaluate the success of memory judgment in humans.

papers.title: Metacognitive domain specificity in feeling-of-knowing but not retrospective confidence
papers.abstract: Previous research has converged on the idea that metacognitive evaluations of memory dissociate between semantic and episodic memory tasks, even if the type of metacognitive judgement is held constant. This often observed difference has been the basis of much theoretical reasoning about the types of cues available when making metacognitive judgements of memory and how metacognition is altered in memory pathologies. Here, we sought to revisit the difference between episodic and semantic feeling-of-knowing (FOK) judgements in the light of recent research which has supported a domain general account of metacognition. One hundred participants performed classical episodic and semantic memory tasks with FOK judgements and confidence judgements. Using the meta-d' framework, we applied a hierarchical Bayesian model to estimate metacognitive sensitivity and cross-task covariance. Results revealed a significant correlation in metacognitive efficiency (meta-d'/d') between the episodic memory task and the semantic memory task for confidence judgements; however, no evidence was found for a cross-task correlation for FOK judgements. This supports the view that FOK judgements are based on different cues in semantic and episodic memory, whereas confidence judgements are domain general.

papers.title: A third kind of episodic memory: Context familiarity is distinct from item familiarity and recollection
papers.abstract: Episodic memory is accounted for with two processes: 'familiarity' when generally recognizing an item and 'recollection' when retrieving the full contextual details bound with the item. Paradoxically, people sometimes report contextual information as familiar but without recollecting details, which is not easily accounted for by existing theories. We tested a combination of item recognition confidence and source memory, focusing upon 'item-only hits with source unknown' ('item familiarity'), 'low-confidence hits with correct source memory' ('context familiarity'), and 'high-confidence hits with correct source memory' ('recollection'). Results across multiple within-subjects (trial-wise) and between subjects (individual variability) levels indicated these were behaviorally and physiologically distinct. Behaviorally, a crossover interaction was evident in response times, with context familiarity being slower than each condition during item recognition, but faster during source memory. Electrophysiologically, a Condition × Time × Location triple dissociation was evident in event-related potentials (ERPs), which was then independently replicated. Context familiarity exhibited an independent negative central effect from 800-1200 ms, differentiated from positive ERPs for item-familiarity (400 to 600 ms) and recollection (600 to 900 ms). These three conditions thus reflect mutually exclusive, fundamentally different processes of episodic memory. Context familiarity is a third distinct process of episodic memory.

papers.title: Subjective Experience of Episodic Memory and Metacognition: A Neurodevelopmental Approach
papers.abstract: Episodic retrieval is characterized by the subjective experience of remembering. This experience enables the co-ordination of memory retrieval processes and can be acted on metacognitively. In successful retrieval, the feeling of remembering may be accompanied by recall of important contextual information. On the other hand, when people fail (or struggle) to retrieve information, other feelings, thoughts, and information may come to mind. In this review, we examine the subjective and metacognitive basis of episodic memory function from a neurodevelopmental perspective, looking at recollection paradigms (such as source memory, and the report of recollective experience) and metacognitive paradigms such as the feeling of knowing). We start by considering healthy development, and provide a brief review of the development of episodic memory, with a particular focus on the ability of children to report first-person experiences of remembering. We then consider neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) such as amnesia acquired in infancy, autism, Williams syndrome, Down syndrome, or 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. This review shows that different episodic processes develop at different rates, and that across a broad set of different NDDs there are various types of episodic memory impairment, each with possibly a different character. This literature is in agreement with the idea that episodic memory is a multifaceted process.

papers.title: True and false memories, parietal cortex, and confidence judgments
papers.abstract: Recent studies have asked whether activity in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and the neocortex can distinguish true memory from false memory. A frequent complication has been that the confidence associated with correct memory judgments (true memory) is typically higher than the confidence associated with incorrect memory judgments (false memory). Accordingly, it has often been difficult to know whether a finding is related to memory confidence or memory accuracy. In the current study, participants made recognition memory judgments with confidence ratings in response to previously studied scenes and novel scenes. The left hippocampus and 16 other brain regions distinguished true and false memories when confidence ratings were different for the two conditions. Only three regions (all in the parietal cortex) distinguished true and false memories when confidence ratings were equated. These findings illustrate the utility of taking confidence ratings into account when identifying brain regions associated with true and false memories. Neural correlates of true and false memories are most easily interpreted when confidence ratings are similar for the two kinds of memories.

papers.title: Unpacking the Medial Temporal Lobe: Separating Recollection and Familiarity
papers.abstract: Our understanding of how the medial temporal lobe (MTL) contributes to human cognition has advanced enormously over the past half a century. My work in the 1990s characterizing the role of recollection and familiarity processes in episodic memory led me to study the MTL's role in these two memory processes. In the current paper, I provide a personal commentary in which I describe the motivating ideas, as well as the invaluable impact of mentors, colleagues, and students that led to a series of studies showing that conscious recollection is critically dependent on the hippocampus, whereas familiarity-based judgments are dependent on regions such as the perirhinal cortex.

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms of Familiarity
papers.abstract: Despite its crucial role in our everyday lives, compared to most other forms of memory, familiarity memory has, over the years, received relatively little targeted attention in the human memory literature. We believe this is because familiarity has predominantly been studied as a comparison condition for recollection, where much more attention has been targeted. The behavioural and neural signatures of familiarity have often been derived from tasks, and under conditions, not optimal for familiarity to be observed or measured in its richest form, or its fullest capacity. We argue here that tests designed specifically to trigger and measure familiarity, reveal a much stronger and more confident form of memory than often assumed. Findings from such methods provide strong confirmation that the hippocampus does not support familiarity memory. Instead, the familiarity memory network includes the medial temporal lobe cortices (MTLc) and amygdala, the thalamus, and prefrontal and parietal cortex. We propose that the material specific MTLc and amygdala regions are responsible for generating familiarity signals, which project via the ventral lateral, and ventral posterior thalamic nuclei, to the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus. This intra-thalamic communication is modulated by familiarity strength. The mediodorsal thalamic nucleus then communicates its familiarity signal to the prefrontal cortex where relative familiarity is computed from independent familiarity and novelty signals. These signals converge in integration regions in both the prefrontal and parietal cortex allowing memory judgements and familiarity decisions to be made. We conclude by highlighting and briefly discussing several key outstanding questions.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Subjective Familiarity and Choice Bias during Episodic Memory Judgments
papers.abstract: Successful recognition memory decisions depend on mnemonic and decision making processes that are computed by multiple, distributed brain areas. However, little is known about what computations these areas perform or how these areas are connected. Here, I collected behavioral and functional magnetic resonance imaging data from humans during the performance of an old-new recognition memory task with retrospective confidence judgments. Across runs, choice bias was successfully manipulated by providing rewards for correct responses that were either symmetric (equal reward for hits and correct rejections) or asymmetric (one response worth more than the other). Successful recognition memory was associated with activation in anterior prefrontal, parahippocampal, posterior cingulate, and parietal cortex. Resting state functional connectivity demonstrated that these brain areas are organized into two distinct networks. The first network includes parahippocampal cortex and angular gyrus. The second network includes lateral prefrontal cortex and intraparietal sulcus. The hippocampal-cortical network was most active during old vs. new decisions, did not differentiate hits from false alarms, and was differentially active during low confidence old and new judgments. In contrast, while the frontoparietal network was robustly activated by hits, it was not activated during either false alarms or low confidence old judgments. Thus, these two distinct networks can be distinguished by their relative connectivity to the medial temporal lobe vs. lateral prefrontal cortex and their responses during uncertain old judgments and errors. The choice bias manipulation had opposing effects on the parietal components of these networks, which further suggests these networks make distinct contributions to mnemonic decision making.

papers.title: Recollection and Familiarity Make Independent Contributions to Memory Judgments
papers.abstract: Recognition memory can be supported by the processes of recollection and familiarity. Recollection is recovery of qualitative information about a prior event. Familiarity is a scalar strength signal that permits judgments of prior occurrence. There is vigorous debate about how these processes are conceptualized, how they contribute to memory judgments, and which brain regions support them. One popular method for investigating these questions is the Remember/Know procedure, where subjects give a Remember response to studied stimuli for which they can recover contextual details of the study encounter, and a Know response when details are not recovered but subjects nevertheless believe that a stimulus was studied. According to one model, Remember responses are strong memories that are typically associated with relatively high levels of recollection and familiarity. Know responses are weaker memories and are typically associated with lower levels of both processes. Data inconsistent with this account were obtained in this experiment, where magnetoencephalographic (MEG) measures of neural activity were acquired in the test phase of a verbal memory task where healthy human volunteers made Remember, Know, or New judgments to studied and unstudied words. An MEG index of the process of recollection was larger for Remember than Know judgments, whereas the reverse was true for a MEG index of familiarity. Critically, this result is predicted by a model where recollection and familiarity make independent contributions to Remember and Know judgments, and provides a powerful constraint when mapping memory processes onto their neural substrates.

papers.title: Recognition memory and the hippocampus: A test of the hippocampal contribution to recollection and familiarity
papers.abstract: It has been suggested that the hippocampus selectively supports recollection and that adjacent cortex in the medial temporal lobe can support familiarity. Alternatively, it has been suggested that the hippocampus supports both recollection and familiarity. We tested these suggestions by assessing the performance of patients with hippocampal lesions on recognition memory tests that differ in the extent to which recollection and familiarity contribute to the recognition decision. When targets and foils are highly similar, prior evidence suggests that, on a forced-choice test in which targets are presented together with highly similar, corresponding foils (the FC-C format), performance is supported primarily by familiarity. By contrast, when targets are presented together with foils that are similar to other targets (the FC-NC format) or when memory is tested in a yes/no (Y/N) format, performance is based much more strongly on recollection. Accordingly, a finding that hippocampal damage impaired both Y/N recognition and FC-NC recognition but spared FC-C recognition would suggest that the hippocampus selectively supports recollection. We administered Y/N, FC-C, and FC-NC tests to five memory-impaired patients with circumscribed hippocampal lesions and 14 controls. The patients were impaired on all three types of recognition test, and there was no indication that the patients were disproportionately benefited or disproportionately impaired on any test. This pattern of performance suggests that the hippocampus supports both recollection and familiarity.

papers.title: Integrating Incremental Learning and Episodic Memory Models of the Hippocampal Region.
papers.abstract: By integrating previous computational models of corticohippocampal function, the authors develop and test a unified theory of the neural substrates of familiarity, recollection, and classical conditioning. This approach integrates models from 2 traditions of hippocampal modeling, those of episodic memory and incremental learning, by drawing on an earlier mathematical model of conditioning, SOP (A. Wagner, 1981). The model describes how a familiarity signal may arise from parahippocampal cortices, giving a novel explanation for the finding that the neural response to a stimulus in these regions decreases with increasing stimulus familiarity. Recollection is ascribed to the hippocampus proper. It is shown how the properties of episodic representations in the neocortex, parahippocampal gyrus, and hippocampus proper may explain phenomena in classical conditioning.
