papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Do All Autoregressive Transformers Remember Facts the Same Way? A Cross-Architecture Analysis of Recall Mechanisms
papers.research_question: Do findings on factual recall mechanisms in GPT-style models generalize across different autoregressive Transformer architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that factual recall mechanisms differ across autoregressive Transformer architectures, with Qwen-based models relying more on Attention modules compared to GPT-based models which use MLP modules.
papers.conclusion: Architectural variations in autoregressive Transformers lead to different mechanisms of factual recall, emphasizing the need for architecture-aware approaches in model editing and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
In GPT-based models, MLP modules in early layers play a key role in storing factual associations.
In Qwen-based models, early Attention layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules.
Gini coefficient analysis shows that Attention modules in Qwen models have concentrated effects on factual recall.
Semantic similarity-based evaluation confirms the differential contributions of Attention and MLP modules across architectures.
The severing effects method has limitations in accurately reflecting the contribution of Attention modules to factual recall.
papers.limitation:
the internal mechanisms by which factual associations are recalled during inference remain insufficiently understood
how factual associations are dynamically accessed across different architectures remains unclear
the interpretation of such structural differences is limited
papers.abstract: Understanding how Transformer-based language models store and retrieve factual associations is critical for improving interpretability and enabling targeted model editing. Prior work, primarily on GPT-style models, has identified MLP modules in early layers as key contributors to factual recall. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize across different autoregressive architectures. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of factual recall across several models -- including GPT, LLaMA, Qwen, and DeepSeek -- analyzing where and how factual information is encoded and accessed. Consequently, we find that Qwen-based models behave differently from previous patterns: attention modules in the earliest layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules. Our findings suggest that even within the autoregressive Transformer family, architectural variations can lead to fundamentally different mechanisms of factual recall.

papers.title: Probing Latent Knowledge Conflict for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How can we improve contextual faithfulness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by moving beyond black-box interventions and analyzing the model's internal reasoning process? Specifically, how is conflict represented in the model's latent space and how does it disrupt faithful generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ProbeRAG, a framework that leverages latent probing to detect knowledge conflicts in the model's hidden states and uses conflict-aware attention modulation to improve contextual faithfulness in RAG systems.
papers.conclusion: ProbeRAG effectively improves contextual faithfulness in RAG by moving beyond black-box interventions to internal guidance, demonstrating consistent and robust performance across various models and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting and aligned knowledge states are linearly separable in the model's latent space, providing a detectable 'conflict feature'.
Contextual noise systematically increases the entropy of these representations, obscuring the conflict feature.
ProbeRAG, which integrates fine-grained knowledge pruning, latent conflict probing, and conflict-aware attention, substantially improves accuracy and contextual faithfulness across multiple benchmarks and models.
The accuracy of the conflict probe is positively correlated with the model's ability to generate faithful responses.
Attention visualization shows that after training with the attention-guidance loss, the model allocates more attention to tokens marked as conflicting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to enhance the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing RAG systems often suffer from an unfaithfulness issue, where the model's response contradicts evidence from the retrieved context. Existing approaches to improving contextual faithfulness largely rely on external interventions, such as prompt engineering, decoding constraints, or reward-based fine-tuning. These works treat the LLM as a black box and overlook a crucial question: how does the LLM internally integrate retrieved evidence with its parametric memory, particularly under knowledge conflicts? To address this gap, we conduct a probing-based analysis of hidden-state representations in LLMs and observe three findings: knowledge integration occurs hierarchically, conflicts manifest as latent signals at the sentence level, and irrelevant context is often amplified when aligned with parametric knowledge. Building on these findings, we propose CLEAR (Conflict-Localized and Enhanced Attention for RAG), a framework that (i) decomposes context into fine-grained sentence-level knowledge, (ii) employs hidden-state probing to localize conflicting knowledge, and (iii) introduces conflict-aware fine-tuning to guide the model to accurately integrate retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR substantially improves both accuracy and contextual faithfulness, consistently outperforming strong baselines under diverse conflict conditions. The related resources are available at https://github.com/LinfengGao/CLEAR.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models, and what are the properties of the neurons that store such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization in multilingual PLMs, and discovers two new types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons.
papers.conclusion: The AMIG method effectively localizes knowledge neurons in multilingual PLMs, and the discoveries of language-independent and degenerate knowledge neurons shed light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed AMIG method localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than baseline methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons exist, are concentrated in the final layers, and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist, exhibit functional overlap, and can be used to help PLMs detect wrong facts in a fact-checking task.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models (BERT and GPT-2).
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration on knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: Aspects of human memory and Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and are these properties due to architectural biases or learned from training data?
papers.core_contribution: Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and these properties are likely learned from the statistical patterns in training data rather than being inherent to the transformer architecture.
papers.conclusion: The human-like memory properties observed in Large Language Models are likely learned from statistical patterns in human-generated text, suggesting that human memory characteristics influence the structure of narratives.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit primacy and recency effects in memory recall.
Adding elaborations to facts improves recall accuracy.
Forgetting in LLMs occurs primarily through interference rather than memory decay.
Repetitions improve recall, with spaced repetitions being more effective than immediate ones.
LLMs show a 'memory formation time' where recall improves with initial distance from the presented facts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are huge artificial neural networks which primarily serve to generate text, but also provide a very sophisticated probabilistic model of language use. Since generating a semantically consistent text requires a form of effective memory, we investigate the memory properties of LLMs and find surprising similarities with key characteristics of human memory. We argue that the human-like memory properties of the Large Language Model do not follow automatically from the LLM architecture but are rather learned from the statistics of the training textual data. These results strongly suggest that the biological features of human memory leave an imprint on the way that we structure our textual narratives.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from The Encoding Specificity Principle
papers.research_question: How do attention layers in transformer-based LLMs implement memory retrieval mechanisms, and are contextual cues represented as keywords?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval, with Q, K, V playing distinct roles analogous to human memory, and that contextual cues are represented as keywords.
papers.conclusion: Attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval mechanisms guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, with keywords serving as retrieval cues and specific neurons encoding these cues.
papers.key_findings:
Swapping V alone induces hallucinations, indicating V stores content.
Swapping both K and V induces systematic hallucination, showing content-addressable matching and content retrieval.
Swapping K only hinders factual recall, representing retrieval failure.
Consistent, model-specific attention neurons are activated by keywords.
Perturbing keywords at the K matrix impairs memory retrieval.
papers.abstract: While explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for large language models (LLMs) remains an evolving field with many unresolved questions, increasing regulatory pressures have spurred interest in its role in ensuring transparency, accountability, and privacy-preserving machine unlearning. Despite recent advances in XAI have provided some insights, the specific role of attention layers in transformer based LLMs remains underexplored. This study investigates the memory mechanisms instantiated by attention layers, drawing on prior research in psychology and computational psycholinguistics that links Transformer attention to cue based retrieval in human memory. In this view, queries encode the retrieval context, keys index candidate memory traces, attention weights quantify cue trace similarity, and values carry the encoded content, jointly enabling the construction of a context representation that precedes and facilitates memory retrieval. Guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, we hypothesize that the cues used in the initial stage of retrieval are instantiated as keywords. We provide converging evidence for this keywords-as-cues hypothesis. In addition, we isolate neurons within attention layers whose activations selectively encode and facilitate the retrieval of context-defining keywords. Consequently, these keywords can be extracted from identified neurons and further contribute to downstream applications such as unlearning.

papers.title: A model of semantic completion in generative episodic memory
papers.research_question: How can episodic memory be modeled as a generative process where an incomplete memory trace is stored and missing information is filled in via semantic completion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a computational model for generative episodic memory that combines a VQ-VAE for compression and a PixelCNN for semantic completion, demonstrating how incomplete memory traces can be filled in to reconstruct plausible episodes.
papers.conclusion: The presented model advances the understanding of generative episodic memory by demonstrating how semantic completion can fill in missing information from incomplete memory traces, aligning with a conceptual framework of episodic memory as a constructive process.
papers.key_findings:
The model can complete missing parts of a memory trace in a semantically plausible way, even generating plausible images from scratch.
The model generalizes well to images not seen during training (e.g., from MNIST digits 0-4 to digits 5-9 and Fashion MNIST).
Compression by the VQ-VAE and semantic completion by the PixelCNN together reduce memory requirements and improve robustness to noise.
The model reproduces key experimental findings: congruent contexts are recalled better than incongruent ones, attention improves memory accuracy, and incorrectly recalled contexts are more often semantically congruent than completely wrong.
Semantic learning within the VQ-VAE (via autoencoding and quantization) contributes to noise reduction and improved classification performance.
papers.limitation:
The attentional selection is rather limited (only row-wise selection of the index matrix).
The index matrix, on which selection and semantic completion are done, is not hierarchical.
The storage process in the hippocampus is not modeled at all.
Due to available degrees of freedom in tuning, the model does not yet have strong explanatory power.
future_direction: Make the attentional selection more flexible.
Adopt a hierarchical version of the VQ-VAE to apply semantic completion to a truly hierarchical representation.
Add a model for one-shot storage of pattern sequences in hippocampal memory to investigate sequential episodes.
papers.abstract: Many different studies have suggested that episodic memory is a generative process, but most computational models adopt a storage view. In this work, we propose a computational model for generative episodic memory. It is based on the central hypothesis that the hippocampus stores and retrieves selected aspects of an episode as a memory trace, which is necessarily incomplete. At recall, the neocortex reasonably fills in the missing information based on general semantic information in a process we call semantic completion. As episodes we use images of digits (MNIST) augmented by different backgrounds representing context. Our model is based on a VQ-VAE which generates a compressed latent representation in form of an index matrix, which still has some spatial resolution. We assume that attention selects some part of the index matrix while others are discarded, this then represents the gist of the episode and is stored as a memory trace. At recall the missing parts are filled in by a PixelCNN, modeling semantic completion, and the completed index matrix is then decoded into a full image by the VQ-VAE. The model is able to complete missing parts of a memory trace in a semantically plausible way up to the point where it can generate plausible images from scratch. Due to the combinatorics in the index matrix, the model generalizes well to images not trained on. Compression as well as semantic completion contribute to a strong reduction in memory requirements and robustness to noise. Finally we also model an episodic memory experiment and can reproduce that semantically congruent contexts are always recalled better than incongruent ones, high attention levels improve memory accuracy in both cases, and contexts that are not remembered correctly are more often remembered semantically congruently than completely wrong.

papers.title: Brain-Language Model Alignment: Insights into the Platonic Hypothesis and Intermediate-Layer Advantage
papers.research_question: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? The paper reviews evidence to test the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.core_contribution: This review of 25 fMRI-based studies provides converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.conclusion: Framing alignment through the dual lenses of the PRH and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage provides a theoretical scaffold for designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment tends to be stronger for larger, higher-performing models and those trained on more tasks, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Cross-modal training reliably enhances alignment by pushing models toward modality-independent conceptual representations.
Intermediate layers of language models show the strongest alignment with brain activity, supporting the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
Fine-tuning (including instruction-tuning and brain-tuning) can improve alignment, but the evidence is not uniformly positive.
Multimodal models, especially vision-language models, align better with brain activity than unimodal models.
papers.limitation: The studies analysed differ in metrics, datasets, and alignment protocols. Such heterogeneity implies that effects of scale or layer depth should be treated as qualitative patterns rather than quantitative laws.
future_direction: Designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.abstract: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? Recent years have seen a rise in studies of neural activations and model alignment. In this work, we review 25 fMRI-based studies published between 2023 and 2025 and explicitly confront their findings with two key hypotheses: (i) the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- that as models scale and improve, they converge to a representation of the real world, and (ii) the Intermediate-Layer Advantage -- that intermediate (mid-depth) layers often encode richer, more generalizable features. Our findings provide converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting both hypotheses and motivating further research on brain-model alignment.

papers.title: Revealing the Deceptiveness of Knowledge Editing: A Mechanistic Analysis of Superficial Editing
papers.research_question: Why do knowledge-edited language models revert to their original knowledge when presented with carefully crafted prompts (attack probes), despite appearing successfully edited according to conventional metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of superficial editing, provides evaluation datasets and metrics, and identifies two key mechanistic factors: the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and specific attention modules in later layers, showing that specific attention heads and their left singular vectors encode original knowledge and cause superficial editing.
papers.conclusion: Superficial editing is a significant challenge for knowledge editing, and the mechanistic analysis reveals the underlying factors in the residual stream and attention modules, with broader applicability to unlearning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect conventional metrics but are vulnerable to attack probes, exhibiting superficial editing in over 70% of cases for some methods.
The residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers shows inhibited enrichment of new knowledge and limited accumulation of original knowledge.
Later attention modules cause the Reversal of the Residual Stream (RRS) phenomenon by incorporating original knowledge into the last position, leading to superficial editing.
Specific attention heads in later layers and their left singular vectors are causally responsible for encoding original knowledge and inducing superficial editing.
Similar patterns are observed in superficial unlearning, demonstrating the generality of the findings.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing, which aims to update the knowledge encoded in language models, can be deceptive. Despite the fact that many existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect performance on conventional metrics, the models edited by them are still prone to generating original knowledge. This paper introduces the concept of "superficial editing" to describe this phenomenon. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that this issue presents a significant challenge to existing algorithms. Through systematic investigation, we identify and validate two key factors contributing to this issue: (1) the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and (2) specific attention modules in later layers. Notably, certain attention heads in later layers, along with specific left singular vectors in their output matrices, encapsulate the original knowledge and exhibit a causal relationship with superficial editing. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the task of superficial unlearning, where we observe consistent patterns in the behavior of specific attention heads and their corresponding left singular vectors, thereby demonstrating the robustness and broader applicability of our methodology and conclusions. Our code is available here.

papers.title: Localized Definitions and Distributed Reasoning: A Proof-of-Concept Mechanistic Interpretability Study via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How is knowledge representation localized in fine-tuned language models, and how does it vary with task complexity?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that factual knowledge is localized while associative knowledge is distributed in fine-tuned models, and introduces CLAP for causal layer attribution.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is localized while associative reasoning depends on distributed intermediate representations, highlighting task-dependent knowledge organization.
papers.key_findings:
Patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference for associative knowledge, indicating distributed representations.
Patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery) for definitional knowledge, indicating localized representation.
Minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning.
Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01).
Editing efficacy depends on task type, with factual knowledge more localized and associative knowledge depending on distributed representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focused exclusively on PubMed epilepsy-related abstracts, potentially limiting generalizability to broader knowledge tasks.
Activation patching may generate false positives due to indirect causal pathways.
Exclusive focus on GPT-2 leaves open questions about scalability to other architectures.
future_direction: Cross-domain comparisons to better understand task-dependent representation patterns.
Methodological integration to improve efficiency.
Extensions to multimodal models where knowledge distribution mechanisms may differ significantly.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the localization of knowledge representation in fine-tuned GPT-2 models using Causal Layer Attribution via Activation Patching (CLAP), a method that identifies critical neural layers responsible for correct answer generation. The model was fine-tuned on 9,958 PubMed abstracts (epilepsy: 20,595 mentions, EEG: 11,674 mentions, seizure: 13,921 mentions) using two configurations with validation loss monitoring for early stopping. CLAP involved (1) caching clean (correct answer) and corrupted (incorrect answer) activations, (2) computing logit difference to quantify model preference, and (3) patching corrupted activations with clean ones to assess recovery. Results revealed three findings: First, patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference, demonstrating that associative knowledge is distributed across multiple layers. Second, patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery), indicating that definitional knowledge is localised. The stronger clean logit difference for definitional questions further supports this localized representation. Third, minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning. Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01). These findings demonstrate that factual knowledge is more localized and associative knowledge depends on distributed representations. We also showed that editing efficacy depends on task type. Our findings not only reconcile conflicting observations about localization in model editing but also emphasize on using task-adaptive techniques for reliable, interpretable updates.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Recognition, recall, and retention of few-shot memories in large language models
papers.research_question: What exactly can a language model remember about training examples that it sees only a few times? How long does that memory persist as the model is continued to be trained with new examples?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models can quickly memorize training examples with few exposures, but these memories are rapidly overwritten during continued training, though some residual memory persists. Recognition memory is more robust than recall and exceeds human performance.
papers.conclusion: Large language models are remarkably effective at fast memorization, but retention is a key challenge; improving retention might alleviate issues like hallucination, though perfect retention may not be desirable for generalization.
papers.key_findings:
A single exposure is sufficient for near-perfect recognition accuracy across various stimulus types, even for challenging distinctions like paraphrases.
Recall requires more exposures (typically 3) to achieve near-perfect performance, especially for natural language sentences.
Memory retention declines rapidly in the first few training updates with new data, then more gradually, with some memories persisting even after 100K updates.
Recognition memory is more robust to interference from new training than recall memory.
Memory for natural language sentences is superior to memory for structureless stimuli like random word sequences or random strings.
papers.limitation:
Need to evaluate bigger, more capable models beyond the 13B parameter models studied.
Limited experimental probes of memory, relying only on recognition tests and conditional recall with greedy decoding, which may be too stringent.
future_direction: Investigate whether ideas from continual learning can improve memory retention in neural networks.
Use more fine-grained measures of memory, such as sampling at different temperatures instead of greedy decoding.
Explore how instruction tuning affects memory properties of language models.
papers.abstract: The training of modern large language models (LLMs) takes place in a regime where most training examples are seen only a few times by the model during the course of training. What does a model remember about such examples seen only a few times during training and how long does that memory persist in the face of continuous training with new examples? Here, we investigate these questions through simple recognition, recall, and retention experiments with LLMs. In recognition experiments, we ask if the model can distinguish the seen example from a novel example; in recall experiments, we ask if the model can correctly recall the seen example when cued by a part of it; and in retention experiments, we periodically probe the model's memory for the original examples as the model is trained continuously with new examples. We find that a single exposure is generally sufficient for a model to achieve near perfect accuracy even in very challenging recognition experiments. We estimate that the recognition performance of even small language models easily exceeds human recognition performance reported in similar experiments with humans (Shepard, 1967). Achieving near perfect recall takes more exposures, but most models can do it in just 3 exposures. The flip side of this remarkable capacity for fast learning is that precise memories are quickly overwritten: recall performance for the original examples drops steeply over the first 10 training updates with new examples, followed by a more gradual decline. Even after 100K updates, however, some of the original examples are still recalled near perfectly. A qualitatively similar retention pattern has been observed in human long-term memory retention studies before (Bahrick, 1984). Finally, recognition is much more robust to interference than recall and memory for natural language sentences is generally superior to memory for stimuli without structure.

papers.title: One SPACE to Rule Them All: Jointly Mitigating Factuality and Faithfulness Hallucinations in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we jointly mitigate factuality and faithfulness hallucinations in LLMs by editing shared activation subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SPACE, a unified framework that jointly enhances factuality and faithfulness in LLMs by identifying and editing shared activation subspaces, mitigating the trade-off between the two types of hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: SPACE effectively mitigates both factuality and faithfulness hallucinations by editing shared activation subspaces, and extensive experiments validate its superiority over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Existing methods for mitigating factuality and faithfulness hallucinations exhibit a trade-off, where improving one degrades the other.
Activation subspaces for factuality and faithfulness hallucinations overlap in LLMs, providing an opportunity for joint mitigation.
SPACE effectively identifies and edits the shared activation subspace, leading to simultaneous improvements in both factuality and faithfulness.
SPACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple benchmarks and model architectures.
The method generalizes well across different model architectures, demonstrating its robustness.
papers.limitation: SPACE's effectiveness is constrained by limitations intrinsic to decoding-level interventions; it cannot remedy factual inaccuracies inherited from pretraining data nor fully resolve deficiencies in handling long-context reasoning.
papers.abstract: LLMs have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities in natural language processing, yet their practical deployment remains hindered by persistent factuality and faithfulness hallucinations. While existing methods address these hallucination types independently, they inadvertently induce performance trade-offs, as interventions targeting one type often exacerbate the other. Through empirical and theoretical analysis of activation space dynamics in LLMs, we reveal that these hallucination categories share overlapping subspaces within neural representations, presenting an opportunity for concurrent mitigation. To harness this insight, we propose SPACE, a unified framework that jointly enhances factuality and faithfulness by editing shared activation subspaces. SPACE establishes a geometric foundation for shared subspace existence through dual-task feature modeling, then identifies and edits these subspaces via a hybrid probe strategy combining spectral clustering and attention head saliency scoring. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Think Like the Brain? Sentence-Level Evidences from Layer-Wise Embeddings and fMRI
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the similarity between LLM representations and human brain activity is due to model scaling or deeper alignment with human language processing principles.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that instruction tuning and semantic comprehension ability, rather than model scale alone, drive the alignment between LLM representations and human brain activity during sentence processing.
papers.conclusion: Instruction tuning and semantic comprehension capacity, not merely parameter size, are key drivers of neural similarity, and the alignment is anatomically and functionally specific to intermediate layers and hemispheric specializations.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of LLMs show higher correlation with brain activity than final layers.
Instruction-tuned models exhibit better performance and stronger neural alignment compared to their base versions.
Hemispheric asymmetry in brain regions aligns with functional specialization, with left-hemisphere regions correlating more with core language processing and right-hemisphere regions with higher cognitive functions.
future_direction: Training procedures that explicitly target alignment with brain data to produce more cognitively plausible models.
Developing hybrid neuro-symbolic LLMs to better reflect distributed and lateralized processing patterns observed in the brain.
papers.abstract: Understanding whether large language models (LLMs) and the human brain converge on similar computational principles remains a fundamental and important question in cognitive neuroscience and AI. Do the brain-like patterns observed in LLMs emerge simply from scaling, or do they reflect deeper alignment with the architecture of human language processing? This study focuses on the sentence-level neural mechanisms of language models, systematically investigating how layer-wise representations in LLMs align with the dynamic neural responses during human sentence comprehension. By comparing hierarchical embeddings from 14 publicly available LLMs with fMRI data collected from participants, who were exposed to a naturalistic narrative story, we constructed sentence-level neural prediction models to identify the model layers most significantly correlated with brain region activations. Results show that improvements in model performance drive the evolution of representational architectures toward brain-like hierarchies, particularly achieving stronger functional and anatomical correspondence at higher semantic abstraction levels. These findings advance our understanding of the computational parallels between LLMs and the human brain, highlighting the potential of LLMs as models for human language processing.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: On the Behavior of Convolutional Nets for Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How discriminative are individual CNN features for characterizing classes across different datasets, and how can they be used for knowledge representation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a statistical analysis of individual CNN features for feature extraction, showing that features can be discriminative by both their presence and absence, and that convolutional features are more general and discriminant than previously thought, enabling their use for knowledge representation without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: CNN features, especially from convolutional layers, are highly discriminative and can be used for knowledge representation by both presence and absence, with context being key in the feature extraction process.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be characteristic of a class by their presence or their absence, providing two modalities of information.
Convolutional features are more general and discriminant than previously considered, opening their use for knowledge representation and unsupervised learning.
Low and middle level features behave similarly across datasets, indicating they can be used for knowledge representation on a wide variety of datasets without fine-tuning.
The relevance of fully-connected features is strongly tied to the similarity between the source and target tasks; for dissimilar tasks, they behave similarly to convolutional features.
A thresholding method based on statistical distance can be applied to remove noisy features, with the threshold correlated to the number of images per class.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are representation learning techniques. During training, a deep net is capable of generating a descriptive language of unprecedented size and detail in machine learning. Extracting the descriptive language coded within a trained CNN model (in the case of image data), and reusing it for other purposes is a field of interest, as it provides access to the visual descriptors previously learnt by the CNN after processing millions of images, without requiring an expensive training phase. Contributions to this field (commonly known as feature representation transfer or transfer learning) have been purely empirical so far, extracting all CNN features from a single layer close to the output and testing their performance by feeding them to a classifier. This approach has provided consistent results, although its relevance is limited to classification tasks. In a completely different approach, in this paper we statistically measure the discriminative power of every single feature found within a deep CNN, when used for characterizing every class of 11 datasets. We seek to provide new insights into the behavior of CNN features, particularly the ones from convolutional layers, as this can be relevant for their application to knowledge representation and reasoning. Our results confirm that low and middle level features may behave differently to high level features, but only under certain conditions. We find that all CNN features can be used for knowledge representation purposes both by their presence or by their absence, doubling the information a single CNN feature may provide. We also study how much noise these features may include, and propose a thresholding approach to discard most of it. All these insights have a direct application to the generation of CNN embedding spaces.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge acquired during LLM pretraining, and how are LLMs affected by the training data at each step? How do training conditions affect the effectivity of factual knowledge acquisition? How is acquired factual knowledge forgotten, and how does training conditions affect forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during LLM pretraining, revealing that acquisition occurs by accumulating small probability increases with each encounter, but is diluted by subsequent forgetting. It also finds that effectivity does not improve with more pretraining data, but model size helps, and forgetting follows a power-law.
papers.conclusion: Factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining is a process of incremental probability increases countered by forgetting, and this understanding can explain phenomena like poor long-tail knowledge performance and the benefits of deduplication.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge acquisition occurs by accumulating micro-acquisitions (small increases in log probability) with subsequent forgetting each time the model encounters the knowledge during pretraining.
Effectivity (immediate improvement in log probability) does not improve with more pretraining tokens, but does improve with larger model size.
Forgetting of acquired factual knowledge follows a power-law relationship with training steps (or tokens).
Training with duplicated data leads to faster forgetting compared to paraphrased data, highlighting the importance of deduplication.
Training with larger batch sizes makes models more robust to forgetting, enhancing knowledge acquisition.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent observation that large language models (LLMs) can store substantial factual knowledge, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms of how they acquire factual knowledge through pretraining. This work addresses this gap by studying how LLMs acquire factual knowledge during pretraining. The findings reveal several important insights into the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during pretraining. First, counterintuitively, we observe that pretraining on more data shows no significant improvement in the model's capability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. Next, there is a power-law relationship between training steps and forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge, and LLMs trained with duplicated training data exhibit faster forgetting. Third, training LLMs with larger batch sizes can enhance the models' robustness to forgetting. Overall, our observations suggest that factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining occurs by progressively increasing the probability of factual knowledge presented in the pretraining data at each step. However, this increase is diluted by subsequent forgetting. Based on this interpretation, we demonstrate that we can provide plausible explanations for recently observed behaviors of LLMs, such as the poor performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge and the benefits of deduplicating the pretraining corpus.

papers.title: Birds have four legs?! NumerSense: Probing Numerical Commonsense Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Does and to what extent do pre-trained language models capture numerical commonsense knowledge, and how robust is this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing task and dataset (NumerSense) to evaluate numerical commonsense knowledge in pre-trained language models, finding that models perform poorly and are brittle to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Powerful pre-trained models such as BERT and RoBERTa perform surprisingly poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge even after fine-tuning, and the introduced dataset provides a basis for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa perform poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge without fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning with distant supervision improves performance but still far from human performance.
Models are brittle to adversarial examples (e.g., inserting adjectives).
Attention analysis shows that important words for numerical commonsense (subject/object) receive low attention weights.
Open-domain QA models also perform poorly on 'how-many' questions derived from NumerSense.
future_direction: Improving PTLMs' abilities to faithfully capture (numerical) commonsense.
Populating numerical facts in current commonsense knowledge bases.
Improving open-domain QA for 'how-many' questions.
Incorporating more structured inductive biases (e.g., dependencies and semantic roles) in pre-training.
Controlling bias in masked language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent works show that pre-trained language models (PTLMs), such as BERT, possess certain commonsense and factual knowledge. They suggest that it is promising to use PTLMs as "neural knowledge bases" via predicting masked words. Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: Sycophancy Hides Linearly in the Attention Heads
papers.research_question: How are correct-to-incorrect sycophancy signals represented in language models, and can they be steered using linear interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that correct-to-incorrect sycophancy is most linearly separable in a sparse subset of middle-layer attention heads, and that steering these heads with linear interventions effectively reduces sycophantic shifts.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate that attention-level activations are a practical and interpretable locus for mitigating sycophancy with simple, linear interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy signals are detectable and steerable using simple linear probes.
These signals are most linearly separable and steerable in a sparse subset of middle-layer multi-head attention (MHA) heads, compared to the residual stream or MLP layers.
The influential sycophancy heads attend disproportionately to user disagreement tokens and sycophantic expressions in the dialogue.
The sycophancy direction is distinct from the previously identified 'truthful' direction, suggesting factual accuracy and deference resistance arise from related but distinct mechanisms.
Linear interventions on the identified attention heads can mitigate sycophantic behavior while preserving factual accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are restricted to Gemma-3 and Llama-3.2 models.
Focus is primarily on correctness-preserving behavior and direct measures of sycophancy reduction; broader impacts on generation style and other alignment dimensions remain outside the current scope.
Attention patterns are used as diagnostic correlation rather than exhaustive accounts of the decision process.
future_direction: Investigating additional model sizes and architectures.
Studying broader impacts on generation style and other alignment dimensions.
Performing multi-objective steering.
papers.abstract: We find that correct-to-incorrect sycophancy signals are most linearly separable within multi-head attention activations. Motivated by the linear representation hypothesis, we train linear probes across the residual stream, multilayer perceptron (MLP), and attention layers to analyze where these signals emerge. Although separability appears in the residual stream and MLPs, steering using these probes is most effective in a sparse subset of middle-layer attention heads. Using TruthfulQA as the base dataset, we find that probes trained on it transfer effectively to other factual QA benchmarks. Furthermore, comparing our discovered direction to previously identified "truthful" directions reveals limited overlap, suggesting that factual accuracy, and deference resistance, arise from related but distinct mechanisms. Attention-pattern analysis further indicates that the influential heads attend disproportionately to expressions of user doubt, contributing to sycophantic shifts. Overall, these findings suggest that sycophancy can be mitigated through simple, targeted linear interventions that exploit the internal geometry of attention activations.

papers.title: Understanding Gated Neurons in Transformers from Their Input-Output Functionality
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between what a neuron reads and what it writes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parameter-based method to classify gated neurons in transformers by input-output weight similarity, finding that enrichment neurons dominate early-middle layers while depletion neurons are more common in later layers.
papers.conclusion: The input-output perspective complements activation-dependent analyses and approaches that treat input and output separately, providing insights into how neurons manipulate concepts in the residual stream.
papers.key_findings:
Enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers across all 12 models studied, whereas later layers tend more towards depletion neurons.
A large proportion of neurons are input manipulators, with conditional enrichment being the most common class, especially in early-middle layers.
Many neurons exhibit double checking, where gate and input weight vectors are approximately orthogonal but intuitively represent the same concept.
The median cosine similarity between input and output weights is positive in early layers and negative in later layers, indicating a smooth transition in functionality.
Neurons rarely have prototypical weight configurations; instead, they often add novel but related information to the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method is parameter-based and therefore limited in scope; it is not designed to replace other neuron analysis methods.
Mathematical similarities of weights may not reflect semantic similarity; orthogonal vectors can represent similar concepts, and similar vectors can represent non-identical concepts.
Case studies of individual neurons may be cherry-picked, focusing on interpretable neurons in later layers, so interpretations may not generalize.
The paper provides only possible interpretations of observed phenomena, not definitive explanations.
future_direction: Extend the method to non-gated activation functions.
Study the evolution of input-output functionalities during model training.
Go beyond the analysis of single neurons to understand how neurons work together within and across classes.
papers.abstract: Interpretability researchers have attempted to understand MLP neurons of language models based on both the contexts in which they activate and their output weight vectors. They have paid little attention to a complementary aspect: the interactions between input and output. For example, when neurons detect a direction in the input, they might add much the same direction to the residual stream ("enrichment neurons") or reduce its presence ("depletion neurons"). We address this aspect by examining the cosine similarity between input and output weights of a neuron. We apply our method to 12 models and find that enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers whereas later layers tend more towards depletion. To explain this finding, we argue that enrichment neurons are largely responsible for enriching concept representations, one of the first steps of factual recall. Our input-output perspective is a complement to activation-dependent analyses and to approaches that treat input and output separately.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for final predictions in large language models, specifically for knowledge storage?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static neuron-level attribution method based on log probability increase that outperforms other static methods, and uses it to analyze knowledge storage in attention and FFN layers of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate 'query neurons', with analysis on six knowledge types helping to understand LLM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed log probability increase method for neuron attribution achieves superior performance compared to seven other static methods across three metrics (MRR, probability, log probability).
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics (e.g., language, country, city) tends to be stored in the same heads, while knowledge with distinct semantics is stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction, despite many neurons contributing.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which in turn are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B; comparing knowledge storage across different models is essential.
Uses static methods for attribution; comparing with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods is important.
future_direction: Explore other types of knowledge beyond the six studied.
Compare knowledge storage similarities and differences across different models.
Compare static attribution methods with other methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Understanding New-Knowledge-Induced Factual Hallucinations in LLMs: Analysis and Interpretation
papers.research_question: What are the fine-grained manifestations and underlying mechanisms of factual hallucinations induced by fine-tuning LLMs on new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Learning new knowledge during fine-tuning weakens LLMs' attention to key question entities, causing factual hallucinations; injecting a small amount of known knowledge late in training (KnownPatch) restores attention and mitigates hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning on new knowledge induces factual hallucinations by weakening attention to key entities, but this can be mitigated by late-stage injection of known knowledge, which restores attention patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Training on unknown knowledge leads to severe hallucinations in the same knowledge type and also spills over to other types and out-of-domain tasks.
When a knowledge type consists entirely of new knowledge, even a small amount can markedly increase hallucination tendencies.
Learning new knowledge reduces the model's attention to key entities in the question, correlating with hallucination severity.
Injecting known knowledge late in training (KnownPatch) restores attention patterns and mitigates hallucinations.
Hallucinations propagate primarily through lexically similar contexts, not semantic similarity.
papers.limitation: In real-world datasets, it is difficult to control whether knowledge is new to the model because most knowledge may have been seen during pre-training.
papers.abstract: Prior works have shown that fine-tuning on new knowledge can induce factual hallucinations in large language models (LLMs), leading to incorrect outputs when evaluated on previously known information. However, the specific manifestations of such hallucination and its underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Our work addresses this gap by designing a controlled dataset \textit{Biography-Reasoning}, and conducting a fine-grained analysis across multiple knowledge types and two task types, including knowledge question answering (QA) and knowledge reasoning tasks. We find that hallucinations not only severely affect tasks involving newly introduced knowledge, but also propagate to other evaluation tasks. Moreover, when fine-tuning on a dataset in which a specific knowledge type consists entirely of new knowledge, LLMs exhibit elevated hallucination tendencies. This suggests that the degree of unfamiliarity within a particular knowledge type, rather than the overall proportion of new knowledge, is a stronger driver of hallucinations. Through interpretability analysis, we show that learning new knowledge weakens the model's attention to key entities in the input question, leading to an over-reliance on surrounding context and a higher risk of hallucination. Conversely, reintroducing a small amount of known knowledge during the later stages of training restores attention to key entities and substantially mitigates hallucination behavior. Finally, we demonstrate that disrupted attention patterns can propagate across lexically similar contexts, facilitating the spread of hallucinations beyond the original task.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
