Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Unveiling Knowledge Utilization Mechanisms in LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge stream within the RAG framework, and how do LLM modules function in knowledge utilization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unveils the intrinsic knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLMs in RAG scenarios from macroscopic (knowledge streaming) and microscopic (module functions) perspectives, introducing KAPE to identify knowledge-specific neurons and demonstrating how deactivating them can shift the model's reliance between internal and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how LLMs integrate internal and external knowledge in RAG, advancing interpretability and paving the way for designing more efficient and controllable LLM architectures capable of balancing parametric and contextual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge streaming within RAG can be divided into four distinct stages: knowledge refinement, elicitation, expression, and contestation.
The relevance of retrieved passages guides the knowledge streaming, primarily affecting the knowledge elicitation stage.
The proposed KAPE metric can identify neurons associated with internal or external knowledge, and selectively deactivating these neurons can alter the LLM's preference for one knowledge source over the other.
Multi-head attention (MHA) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules have complementary roles: MHA facilitates information integration, while MLP layers help verify knowledge accuracy and are sensitive to factual correctness.
The LLM evaluates the relevance between the query and external knowledge during the knowledge elicitation stage via information flow between them.
future_direction: Future work will focus on refining these mechanisms to improve real-world applications and extend the boundaries of AI-driven knowledge retrieval systems, developing more nuanced models that better handle the complexities of knowledge integration.
papers.abstract: Considering the inherent limitations of parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely employed to expand their knowledge scope. Since RAG has shown promise in knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain question answering, its broader application to complex tasks and intelligent assistants has further advanced its utility. Despite this progress, the underlying knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLM-based RAG remain underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic investigation of the intrinsic mechanisms by which LLMs integrate internal (parametric) and external (retrieved) knowledge in RAG scenarios. Specially, we employ knowledge stream analysis at the macroscopic level, and investigate the function of individual modules at the microscopic level. Drawing on knowledge streaming analyses, we decompose the knowledge utilization process into four distinct stages within LLM layers: knowledge refinement, knowledge elicitation, knowledge expression, and knowledge contestation. We further demonstrate that the relevance of passages guides the streaming of knowledge through these stages. At the module level, we introduce a new method, knowledge activation probability entropy (KAPE) for neuron identification associated with either internal or external knowledge. By selectively deactivating these neurons, we achieve targeted shifts in the LLM's reliance on one knowledge source over the other. Moreover, we discern complementary roles for multi-head attention and multi-layer perceptron layers during knowledge formation. These insights offer a foundation for improving interpretability and reliability in retrieval-augmented LLMs, paving the way for more robust and transparent generative solutions in knowledge-intensive domains.

papers.title: Knowledge Localization: Mission Not Accomplished? Enter Query Localization!
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption hold for all facts? If not, what is a more realistic assumption?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Query Localization (QL) assumption, which includes query-KN mapping and dynamic KN selection, and introduces a Consistency-Aware KN modification method that improves knowledge editing performance.
papers.conclusion: The Query Localization assumption provides a more realistic framework for understanding knowledge storage and expression in LLMs than the Knowledge Localization assumption, and is validated by improved editing performance.
papers.key_findings:
Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) that violates the Knowledge Localization assumption is widespread in LLMs.
For KI, knowledge neurons are associated with specific queries rather than the fact itself (query-KN mapping).
The attention module plays a key role in selecting appropriate knowledge neurons for expression (dynamic KN selection).
The proposed Consistency-Aware KN modification method, based on the QL assumption, improves knowledge editing performance over baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The work primarily focuses on factual knowledge, and it remains unclear whether the QL assumption applies to other types of knowledge.
The distinction between Consistent Knowledge (KC) and Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) might be related to the pre-training process.
future_direction: Exploring how to reconcile the QL assumption with other current theories.
Further utilizing the QL assumption to improve model editing methods.
Integrating the attention module more effectively to develop enhanced methods for dynamically editing knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the mechanisms behind how they store and express this knowledge remain unclear. The Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis is a prominent theory for explaining these mechanisms. This theory is based on the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption, which suggests that a fact can be localized to a few knowledge storage units, namely knowledge neurons. However, this assumption has two limitations: first, it may be too rigid regarding knowledge storage, and second, it neglects the role of the attention module in knowledge expression. In this paper, we first re-examine the KL assumption and demonstrate that its limitations do indeed exist. To address these, we then present two new findings, each targeting one of the limitations: one focusing on knowledge storage and the other on knowledge expression. We summarize these findings as \textbf{Query Localization} (QL) assumption and argue that the KL assumption can be viewed as a simplification of the QL assumption. Based on QL assumption, we further propose the Consistency-Aware KN modification method, which improves the performance of knowledge modification, further validating our new assumption. We conduct 39 sets of experiments, along with additional visualization experiments, to rigorously confirm our conclusions. Code is available at https://github.com/heng840/KnowledgeLocalization.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: Do LLMs dream of elephants (when told not to)? Latent concept association and associative memory in transformers
papers.research_question: How robust is fact retrieval in LLMs to context changes, and what does this reveal about associative memory mechanisms in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that fact retrieval in LLMs is not robust and can be hijacked by context, and proposes a synthetic latent concept association task to show transformers implement associative memory via self-attention for aggregation and the value matrix for memory retrieval.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit associative memory behavior, which makes fact retrieval non-robust, and understanding this can help develop more robust models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are susceptible to context hijacking, where adding context that does not change factual meaning can lead to incorrect fact retrieval.
The latent concept association task models fact retrieval in transformers and shows that transformers can solve it by using self-attention to aggregate information and the value matrix as associative memory.
Theoretical analysis shows that the value matrix is crucial for associative memory and that the embedding space can exhibit a low-rank structure.
In the underparameterized regime, embedding training is necessary for good performance, and the learned embeddings have a structure that relates inner product to Hamming distance.
The attention mechanism can select relevant tokens based on latent clusters, mitigating noise.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to open-source models and may not generalize to commercial models like GPT-4.
The theoretical analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, while multi-layer transformers have more complex behaviors (e.g., induction heads).
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-layer transformers.
Studying more complex associative memory mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have the capacity to store and recall facts. Through experimentation with open-source models, we observe that this ability to retrieve facts can be easily manipulated by changing contexts, even without altering their factual meanings. These findings highlight that LLMs might behave like an associative memory model where certain tokens in the contexts serve as clues to retrieving facts. We mathematically explore this property by studying how transformers, the building blocks of LLMs, can complete such memory tasks. We study a simple latent concept association problem with a one-layer transformer and we show theoretically and empirically that the transformer gathers information using self-attention and uses the value matrix for associative memory.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and is this due to deception or other factors like confabulation and heterogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that most disagreements between LM outputs and internal truthfulness representations are due to confabulation and heterogeneity, with deception being rare, and that probes are better calibrated than queries.
papers.conclusion: Disagreements between internal and external representations of truthfulness are predominantly due to different prediction pathways rather than latent deceptive intent, and the proposed taxonomy helps categorize these mismatches.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries on factual question-answering tasks.
Probes are substantially better calibrated than language model queries.
Most query-probe disagreements arise from confabulation (queries confident but probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), not deception.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can improve accuracy over either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, with deception being more prominent in CREAK.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may not capture the full range of model behavior.
Only linear probes were used, and some information may be encoded non-linearly.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs "lie" or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today's LMs, or can query-probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two. Code is available at github.com/lingo-mit/lm-truthfulness.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we detect and resolve knowledge conflicts in LLMs by steering their internal activations at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in LLM activations, effectively steering knowledge selection behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SPARE offers an effective and efficient way to control knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected in the residual stream of LLMs, especially in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively controls knowledge selection, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
SPARE requires only a small set of SAE features (e.g., <0.05% for Gemma2-9B) for effective control.
The residual stream shows skewed representations when models use contextual knowledge compared to parametric knowledge.
Middle layers are more steerable for knowledge selection behavior.
papers.limitation:
Relies on pre-trained SAEs, which may not be available for all models.
Generalization to other types of tasks or conflicts (e.g., complex reasoning, multi-hop questions) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in binary terms (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), while real-world decisions may require more nuance.
papers.abstract: Yu Zhao, Alessio Devoto, Giwon Hong, Xiaotang Du, Aryo Pradipta Gema, Hongru Wang, Xuanli He, Kam-Fai Wong, Pasquale Minervini. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: How Deep is Love in LLMs' Hearts? Exploring Semantic Size in Human-like Cognition
papers.research_question: This study seeks to investigate whether LLMs exhibit similar tendencies in understanding semantic size as humans, thereby providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of human cognition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that multi-modal training is crucial for LLMs to achieve more human-like understanding of semantic size, and that LLMs, especially multi-modal ones, are influenced by attention-grabbing headlines with larger semantic size, revealing potential biases.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that multi-modal training enhances LLMs' understanding of semantic size, making them more human-like, but also introduces biases similar to humans, such as susceptibility to clickbait headlines.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-modal LLMs align more closely with human metaphorical tendencies compared to their text-only backbone LLMs.
Multi-modal LLMs outperform single-modality LLMs in semantic size classification accuracy, indicating multi-modality plays a critical role.
LLMs, especially MLLMs, show a clear preference for selecting product titles with larger semantic sizes in a controlled shopping scenario.
The findings suggest that human cognition cannot be fully acquired through the language modality alone; real-world, multi-modal experiences are essential.
Multi-modal training enhances LLMs' ability to understand both abstract and concrete concepts from a semantic size perspective.
papers.abstract: How human cognitive abilities are formed has long captivated researchers. However, a significant challenge lies in developing meaningful methods to measure these complex processes. With the advent of large language models (LLMs), which now rival human capabilities in various domains, we are presented with a unique testbed to investigate human cognition through a new lens. Among the many facets of cognition, one particularly crucial aspect is the concept of semantic size, the perceived magnitude of both abstract and concrete words or concepts. This study seeks to investigate whether LLMs exhibit similar tendencies in understanding semantic size, thereby providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of human cognition. We begin by exploring metaphorical reasoning, comparing how LLMs and humans associate abstract words with concrete objects of varying sizes. Next, we examine LLMs' internal representations to evaluate their alignment with human cognitive processes. Our findings reveal that multi-modal training is crucial for LLMs to achieve more human-like understanding, suggesting that real-world, multi-modal experiences are similarly vital for human cognitive development. Lastly, we examine whether LLMs are influenced by attention-grabbing headlines with larger semantic sizes in a real-world web shopping scenario. The results show that multi-modal LLMs are more emotionally engaged in decision-making, but this also introduces potential biases, such as the risk of manipulation through clickbait headlines. Ultimately, this study offers a novel perspective on how LLMs interpret and internalize language, from the smallest concrete objects to the most profound abstract concepts like love. The insights gained not only improve our understanding of LLMs but also provide new avenues for exploring the cognitive abilities that define human intelligence.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: A Unified Representation Underlying the Judgment of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does evaluative judgment in Large Language Models rely on specialized modules or a unified, domain-general resource? Specifically, are diverse evaluative judgments computed along a dominant dimension?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs converge on a domain-general architecture for evaluative judgment, characterized by a Valence-Assent Axis (VAA) that jointly encodes subjective valence and factual assent. This axis subordinates reasoning, steering the model to generate rationales consistent with its evaluative state even at the cost of factual accuracy.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a domain-general architecture for evaluative judgment via a unified Valence-Assent Axis, which promotes coherent judgment but can systematically undermine faithful reasoning, offering a mechanistic account for response bias and hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
A single dominant dimension (the Valence-Assent Axis) in LLMs encodes both subjective valence ('what is good') and factual assent ('what is true').
The VAA generalizes across different judgment tasks (value judgment, sentiment analysis, subjective preference, objective verification).
Direct interventions (steering) along the VAA causally control model outputs in both subjective and objective tasks.
The VAA subordinates reasoning: steering the VAA leads the model to generate rationales (coherent hallucinations) consistent with the steered stance, even when factually incorrect.
The VAA is a shared feature across LLMs of varying architectures and scales (tested on 8 models).
papers.abstract: A central architectural question for both biological and artificial intelligence is whether judgment relies on specialized modules or a unified, domain-general resource. While the discovery of decodable neural representations for distinct concepts in Large Language Models (LLMs) has suggested a modular architecture, whether these representations are truly independent systems remains an open question. Here we provide evidence for a convergent architecture for evaluative judgment. Across a range of LLMs, we find that diverse evaluative judgments are computed along a dominant dimension, which we term the Valence-Assent Axis (VAA). This axis jointly encodes subjective valence ("what is good") and the model's assent to factual claims ("what is true"). Through direct interventions, we demonstrate this axis drives a critical mechanism, which is identified as the subordination of reasoning: the VAA functions as a control signal that steers the generative process to construct a rationale consistent with its evaluative state, even at the cost of factual accuracy. Our discovery offers a mechanistic account for response bias and hallucination, revealing how an architecture that promotes coherent judgment can systematically undermine faithful reasoning.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how language models encode and recall time-specific information, focusing on whether there are specific attention heads dedicated to temporal knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads in language models that encode and recall time-specific knowledge, and shows that ablating them impairs temporal knowledge while leaving other capabilities intact.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Temporal Heads are crucial for temporal knowledge in LLMs, and targeting them can enable precise temporal updates without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal Heads, such as a15.h0 and a18.h3 in Llama2, are identified across multiple models and are crucial for temporal knowledge recall.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal effect on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated for both numerical (e.g., 'In 2004') and textual (e.g., 'In the year...') temporal conditions, indicating they encode a broad temporal dimension.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the activations of these heads, enabling targeted updates.
Backup Temporal Heads exist that can compensate when primary heads are ablated, ensuring model robustness.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs was constrained due to lack of temporal dependencies in options.
EAP-IG does not support models with Grouped-Query Attention, limiting analysis of models like Llama-3.
future_direction: Future work should focus on broader application for enhancing temporal reasoning and time-aware model alignment.
papers.abstract: While the ability of language models to elicit facts has been widely investigated, how they handle temporally changing facts remains underexplored. We discover Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that primarily handle temporal knowledge, through circuit analysis. We confirm that these heads are present across multiple models, though their specific locations may vary, and their responses differ depending on the type of knowledge and its corresponding years. Disabling these heads degrades the model's ability to recall time-specific knowledge while maintaining its general capabilities without compromising time-invariant and question-answering performances. Moreover, the heads are activated not only numeric conditions ("In 2004") but also textual aliases ("In the year ..."), indicating that they encode a temporal dimension beyond simple numerical representation. Furthermore, we expand the potential of our findings by demonstrating how temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the values of these heads.

papers.title: Emergence of Episodic Memory in Transformers: Characterizing Changes in Temporal Structure of Attention Scores During Training
papers.research_question: How do temporal biases (like contiguity, primacy, recency) emerge in attention heads and transformer outputs during training, and how do they relate to human episodic memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers develop temporal biases (contiguity, primacy, recency) in attention heads during training, similar to human episodic memory, and that induction heads are crucial for the contiguity effect.
papers.conclusion: Overall, we showed that tools from cognitive science can be used to better understand learning in transformers, providing valuable insights into the emergence of temporal structure during in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal contiguity, primacy, and recency effects emerge in attention heads during training.
Induction heads are the driving force behind the contiguity effect, and ablating them eliminates the effect in transformer outputs.
The magnitude of positional encoding influences the strength of recency and contiguity effects.
Temporal effects are consistent across model sizes (GPT-2 small and medium).
The time constants for contiguity are short (2-4 lags), indicating limited temporal context retrieval.
papers.limitation: The study uses relatively small models, and methodological differences prevent direct parallels with human memory.
papers.abstract: We investigate in-context temporal biases in attention heads and transformer outputs. Using cognitive science methodologies, we analyze attention scores and outputs of the GPT-2 models of varying sizes. Across attention heads, we observe effects characteristic of human episodic memory, including temporal contiguity, primacy and recency. Transformer outputs demonstrate a tendency toward in-context serial recall. Importantly, this effect is eliminated after the ablation of the induction heads, which are the driving force behind the contiguity effect. Our findings offer insights into how transformers organize information temporally during in-context learning, shedding light on their similarities and differences with human memory and learning.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Understanding Factual Recall in Transformers via Associative Memories
papers.research_question: How do transformers store factual information and what is their storage capacity?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow transformers can achieve near-optimal storage capacity for factual recall by using associative memories in both self-attention and MLP components, with a trade-off between them.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can efficiently store factual information using associative memories implemented in self-attention and MLP components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear and MLP associative memories can store a number of associations proportional to their parameter count.
A one-layer transformer can achieve 100% accuracy on a synthetic factual recall task when either the total self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scale linearly with the number of facts.
The transformer exhibits sequential learning dynamics during training, with an initial 'hallucination' stage.
The storage constructions are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
papers.limitation: The linear associative memory construction requires the association function to be injective for optimal capacity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated an impressive ability to perform factual recall. Prior work has found that transformers trained on factual recall tasks can store information at a rate proportional to their parameter count. In our work, we show that shallow transformers can use a combination of associative memories to obtain such near optimal storage capacity. We begin by proving that the storage capacities of both linear and MLP associative memories scale linearly with parameter count. We next introduce a synthetic factual recall task, and prove that a transformer with a single layer of self-attention followed by an MLP can obtain 100% accuracy on the task whenever either the total number of self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scales (up to log factors) linearly with the number of facts. In particular, the transformer can trade off between using the value matrices or the MLP as an associative memory to store the dataset of facts. We complement these expressivity results with an analysis of the gradient flow trajectory of a simplified linear attention model trained on our factual recall task, where we show that the model exhibits sequential learning behavior.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Online Sentence Parsing: Empirical Evidence, Computational Modelling, and Simulations
papers.research_question: How does memory retrieval work during online sentence parsing, and under what conditions does similarity-based interference occur?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Revision Integrated Cue-Based (RICB) model, which successfully predicts similarity-based interference data in floating quantifier processing, emphasizing structural information and revision.
papers.conclusion: The RICB model accounts for the data and underscores the importance of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during real-time sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
Similarity-based interference was observed in ungrammatical sentences but not in grammatical sentences.
The interference patterns were not consistent with existing theories and models.
The RICB model, which assumes heavy weighting of structural cues and includes revision, predicts the observed data.
The results highlight the central role of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during sentence processing.
papers.limitation:
Detecting similarity-based interference requires large sample sizes, particularly in grammatical sentences.
The patterns of interference were not consistent with existing theories and models.
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper reports two experiments (Experiments 1 and 2) and computational simulations designed to investigate and model memory retrieval processes during real-time sentence processing. Central to this study is the hypothesis that linguistic information serves as a cue to retrieve target representations from memory during dependency formation. The basis for this cue-based memory retrieval stems from research showing that non-target representations that match a set of retrieval cues interfere with target retrieval. The susceptibility to this similarity-based interference has been debated in the sentence processing literature, and various hypotheses and models have been formulated and developed. This issue is addressed empirically in Experiments 1 and 2, which investigated similarity-based interference in sentences with a floating quantifier. Bayesian linear mixed models and Bayes factor analyses suggested similarity-based interference. However, the patterns of interference were not consistent with existing theories and models. To reconcile these findings within the framework of cue-based memory retrieval, this paper implements the Revision Integrated Cue-Based (RICB) model based on the ACT–R architecture. This model assumes that structural information is heavily weighted and incorporates the notions of initial retrieval and revision. The results of the simulations indicate that the RICB model successfully predicts the observed data, highlighting the central role of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during real-time sentence processing.

papers.title: Layer-Order Inversion: Rethinking Latent Multi-Hop Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does latent multi-hop reasoning in LLMs follow hop-aligned circuits? If not, what internal mechanisms support multi-hop reasoning? Why do LLMs fail on multi-hop questions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers layer-order inversion in multi-hop reasoning, where later-hop answer entities become decodable earlier than bridge entities, and proposes a probabilistic recall-and-extract framework to explain this behavior.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies layer-order inversion, challenging hop-aligned circuit hypotheses, and proposes a probabilistic recall-and-extract framework that better explains latent multi-hop reasoning, including prior observations and failure modes.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-order inversion occurs where later-hop entities become decodable earlier than bridge entities, contradicting the hop-aligned circuit hypothesis.
Multi-hop reasoning is better explained by a probabilistic recall-and-extract framework: shallow MLP layers perform probabilistic recall of entities, and deeper attention layers selectively extract answer-relevant knowledge.
The probabilistic framework explains prior observations like hop-aligned circuits (as high-probability paths) and chain-of-thought gains (by enriching context priors).
Multi-hop failures arise from insufficient deeper-hop recall under the full query and insufficient knowledge extraction in deeper attention layers, even when single-hop facts are known.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale models (e.g., 6B and 8B parameters) due to computational constraints.
The analysis of knowledge encoded in attention modules is hypothesis-driven and not comprehensively validated due to limited existing methodologies.
future_direction: Clarify the knowledge encoded within the attention module.
Explore implications for model intervention and knowledge editing.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on multi-hop reasoning, yet how they internally compose multiple facts remains unclear. Recent work proposes \emph{hop-aligned circuit hypothesis}, suggesting that bridge entities are computed sequentially across layers before later-hop answers. Through systematic analyses on real-world multi-hop queries, we show that this hop-aligned assumption does not generalize: later-hop answer entities can become decodable earlier than bridge entities, a phenomenon we call \emph{layer-order inversion}, which strengthens with total hops. To explain this behavior, we propose a \emph{probabilistic recall-and-extract} framework that models multi-hop reasoning as broad probabilistic recall in shallow MLP layers followed by selective extraction in deeper attention layers. This framework is empirically validated through systematic probing analyses, reinterpreting prior layer-wise decoding evidence, explaining chain-of-thought gains, and providing a mechanistic diagnosis of multi-hop failures despite correct single-hop knowledge. Code is available at https://github.com/laquabe/Layer-Order-Inversion.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in multilingual LLMs share similarities with English LLMs but with key differences, such as the role of MLPs in extraction and the composition of relation and language in the last token's function vector.
papers.conclusion: These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies—such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition—that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture.
Subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted.
In decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose relation and language in two separate stages.
MLPs play a more prominent role in extraction in multilingual LLMs compared to English LLMs.
papers.limitation: Excluded languages with too few examples, limiting the analysis to a subset of languages.
future_direction: Developing new methodologies for knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying whether models 'think' in English by examining how the function vector is altered across languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a pervasive 'lookback mechanism' that language models use to track characters' beliefs, and introduces the CausalToM dataset for causal analysis of Theory of Mind.
papers.conclusion: The lookback mechanism is a foundational computation for belief tracking in language models, providing a step toward reverse-engineering Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Language models use a systematic 'lookback mechanism' for belief tracking, which involves recalling important information when needed.
The mechanism uses Ordering IDs (OIs) to bind character-object-state triples in the residual stream of state tokens.
Three key lookbacks are identified: binding lookback (retrieves state OI), answer lookback (retrieves state token), and visibility lookback (updates beliefs based on visibility).
The mechanism generalizes across model scales (70B to 405B) and model families (Llama and Qwen).
The visibility lookback uses a visibility ID to retrieve information about observed characters and update the observing character's beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The visibility lookback mechanism is only partially understood and requires further investigation.
The mechanism does not scale to three characters in the visibility condition.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex scenarios with more characters and objects.
Further investigation of the visibility lookback mechanism.
Applying the lookback mechanism analysis to other tasks and domains.
papers.abstract: How do language models (LMs) represent characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality? This question lies at the heart of understanding the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LMs. We analyze LMs' ability to reason about characters' beliefs using causal mediation and abstraction. We construct a dataset, CausalToM, consisting of simple stories where two characters independently change the state of two objects, potentially unaware of each other's actions. Our investigation uncovers a pervasive algorithmic pattern that we call a lookback mechanism, which enables the LM to recall important information when it becomes necessary. The LM binds each character-object-state triple together by co-locating their reference information, represented as Ordering IDs (OIs), in low-rank subspaces of the state token's residual stream. When asked about a character's beliefs regarding the state of an object, the binding lookback retrieves the correct state OI and then the answer lookback retrieves the corresponding state token. When we introduce text specifying that one character is (not) visible to the other, we find that the LM first generates a visibility ID encoding the relation between the observing and the observed character OIs. In a visibility lookback, this ID is used to retrieve information about the observed character and update the observing character's beliefs. Our work provides insights into belief tracking mechanisms, taking a step toward reverse-engineering ToM reasoning in LMs.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Illustrating a neural model of logic computations: The case of Sherlock Holmes' old maxim
papers.research_question: What is the cognitive reason for the feeling that Holmes' maxim is an evident truth? The paper postulates that it is because our brains have neural modules that perform modal logical computations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a neural model based on matrix associative memories that can perform modal logical computations, explaining why humans accept Sherlock Holmes' maxim as true.
papers.conclusion: Our brains are equipped with neural modules capable of modal logical computations, which explains why we accept Holmes' maxim as true.
papers.key_findings:
The paper provides a neural model based on matrix associative memories that can perform logical operations.
It shows how modal logic operators (possibility and necessity) can be implemented in the model.
It demonstrates how Holmes' maxim can be represented and computed by the model.
It connects the model with subjective probabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical approach helps explain cognitive acceptability, but mathematics itself remains unexplained, making the explanation incomplete and provisional.
The link between cognitive probabilities and formal probabilities is left as an open problem.
future_direction: Exploring whether the process represents a class of nonmonotonic reasoning.
Investigating the link between cognitive probabilities and formal probabilities.
papers.abstract: Natural languages can express some logical propositions that humans are able to understand. We illustrate this fact with a famous text that Conan Doyle attributed to Holmes: 'It is an old maxim of mine that when you have excluded the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth'. This is a subtle logical statement usually felt as an evident truth. The problem we are trying to solve is the cognitive reason for such a feeling. We postulate here that we accept Holmes' maxim as true because our adult brains are equipped with neural modules that naturally perform modal logical computations.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Adaptive Activation Steering: A Tuning-Free LLM Truthfulness Improvement Method for Diverse Hallucinations Categories
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to improve the truthfulness of large language models by adaptively steering activations during inference, addressing the gap between what the model knows and what it tells, and handling diverse hallucination categories.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Adaptive Activation Steering (ACT), a tuning-free method that improves LLM truthfulness by adaptively shifting activations toward truthful directions using diverse steering vectors and adaptive intensity control.
papers.conclusion: ACT is a tuning-free method that enhances LLM truthfulness by steering activations with diverse vectors and adaptive intensity, effectively addressing the gap between knowing and telling, and marks a promising advancement in reliable AI-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
ACT significantly improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA across multiple models (e.g., LLaMA, LLaMA2, Alpaca, Vicuna, LLaMA2-Chat, LLaMA3).
ACT's adaptive intensity control and diverse steering vectors are effective, outperforming existing baselines like ITI, CCS, RepE, and Mean-Centring.
ACT is orthogonal to few-shot prompting and instruction fine-tuning, and can be combined with them for further improvement.
ACT shows scalability across model sizes (7B to 65B), with consistent improvements.
ACT requires only a few dozen training samples and adds constant-time complexity during inference.
papers.limitation:
Applicability in real-world chat settings involving multi-turn conversations has not been fully explored.
The trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness (e.g., the smoothness of generated text) is not explored.
future_direction: Explore ACT in multi-turn conversation settings.
Investigate the trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have indicated that Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor an inherent understanding of truthfulness, yet often fail to consistently express it and generate false statements. This gap between "knowing" and "telling" poses a challenge for ensuring the truthfulness of generated content. Inspired by recent work on the practice of encoding human-interpretable concepts linearly within large language models, we treat truthfulness as a specially linearly encoded concept within LLMs, and introduce Adaptive Activation Steering (ACT), a tuning-free method that adaptively shifts LLM's activations in the "truthful" direction during inference. ACT addresses diverse categories of hallucinations by utilizing diverse truthfulness-related steering vectors and adjusting the steering intensity adaptively. Applied as an add-on across various models, ACT significantly improves truthfulness in LLaMA ($\uparrow$ 142%), LLaMA2 ($\uparrow$ 24%), Alpaca ($\uparrow$ 36%), Vicuna ($\uparrow$ 28%), LLaMA2-Chat ($\uparrow$ 19%), and LLaMA3($\uparrow$ 34%). Furthermore, we verify ACT's scalability across larger models (13B, 33B, 65B), underscoring the adaptability of ACT to large-scale language models. Our code is available at https://github.com/tianlwang/ACT.

papers.title: Attention Sinks: A 'Catch, Tag, Release' Mechanism for Embeddings
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why attention sinks emerge in later tokens, whether they encode semantically meaningful information, how they differ between pretrained and reasoning models, and the impact of query-key normalization on attention sinks.
papers.core_contribution: This paper uncovers the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism in LLMs, where attention sinks catch tokens, tag them with semantically meaningful information, and release the tags into the residual stream for later use. The mechanism is prevalent across model families, more pronounced in reasoning models, and persists despite query-key normalization.
